Compare <reference osisRef="Jas.1.1">Jas 1:1</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.1">1Pe 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.2">Jas 1:2</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.6">1Pe 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.12">4:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.11">Jas 1:11</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.24">1Pe 1:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.18">Jas 1:18</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.3">1Pe 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.2.7">Jas 2:7</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.14">1Pe 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.3.13">Jas 3:13</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.12">1Pe 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.1">Jas 4:1</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.11">1Pe 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.6">Jas 4:6</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.5">1Pe 5:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.7">Jas 4:7</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.6">1Pe 5:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.10">Jas 4:10</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.6">1Pe 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.20">Jas 5:20</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.6">1Pe 4:6</reference>. Its being written in the purest Greek shows it was intended not only for the Jews at Jerusalem, but also for the Hellenistic, that is, Greek-speaking, Jews.<div eID="gen39363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39364" type="x-p"/> The style is close, curt, and sententious, gnome following after gnome. A Hebraic character pervades the Epistle, as appears in the occasional poetic parallelisms (<reference osisRef="Jas.3.1-Jas.3.12">Jas 3:1-12</reference>). Compare "assembly": Greek, "synagogue," <reference osisRef="Jas.2.2">Jas 2:2</reference>, Margin. The images are analogical arguments, combining at once logic and poetry. Eloquence and persuasiveness are prominent characteristics.<div eID="gen39364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39365" type="x-p"/> The similarity to Matthew, the most Hebrew of the Gospels, is just what we might expect from the bishop of Jerusalem writing to Israelites. In it the higher spirit of Christianity is seen putting the Jewish law in its proper place. The law is enforced in its everlasting spirit, not in the letter for which the Jews were so zealous. The doctrines of grace, the distinguishing features of Paul's teaching to the Hellenists and Gentiles, are less prominent as being already taught by that apostle. James complements Paul's teaching, and shows to the Jewish Christians who still kept the legal ordinances down to the fall of Jerusalem, the spiritual principle of the law, namely, love manifested in obedience. To sketch "the perfect man" continuing in the Gospel law of liberty, is his theme.<div eID="gen39365" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jas.1.1-Jas.1.27">Jas 1:1-27</reference>. Inscription: Exhortation on Hearing, Speaking, and Wrath.</title> <div sID="gen39366" type="x-p"/> The last subject is discussed in <reference osisRef="Jas.3.13-Jas.4.17">Jas 3:13-4:17</reference>.<div eID="gen39366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39367" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18620"/><hi type="bold">1. James--</hi>an apostle of the circumcision, with Peter and John, James in Jerusalem, Palestine, and Syria; Peter in Babylon and the East; John in Ephesus and Asia Minor. Peter addresses the dispersed Jews of Pontus, Galatia, and Cappadocia; James, the Israelites of the twelve tribes scattered abroad.<div eID="gen39367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39368" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">servant of God--</hi>not that he was not an apostle; for Paul, an apostle, also calls himself so; but as addressing the Israelites generally, including even indirectly the unbelieving, he in humility omits the title "apostle"; so Paul in writing to the Hebrews; similarly Jude, an apostle, in his General Epistle.<div eID="gen39368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39369" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jesus Christ--</hi>not mentioned again save in <reference osisRef="Jas.2.1">Jas 2:1</reference>; not at all in his speeches (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.14">Ac 15:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.21.20">21:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.21.21">21</reference>), lest his introducing the name of Jesus oftener should seem to arise from vanity, as being "the Lord's brother" [Bengel]. His teaching being practical, rather than doctrinal, required less frequent mention of Christ's name.<div eID="gen39369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39370" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scattered abroad--</hi>literally "which are in the dispersion." The dispersion of the Israelites, and their connection with Jerusalem as a center of religion, was a divinely ordered means of propagating Christianity. The pilgrim troops of the law became caravans of the Gospel [Wordsworth].<div eID="gen39370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39371" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">greeting--</hi>found in no other Christian letter, but in James and the Jerusalem Synod's Epistle to the Gentile churches; an undesigned coincidence and mark or genuineness. In the original Greek (chairein) for "greeting," there is a connection with the "joy" to which they are exhorted amidst their existing distresses from poverty and consequent oppression. Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.15.26">Ro 15:26</reference>, which alludes to their poverty. <div eID="gen39371" type="x-p"/>
entries.243f8aa53b972e37fd1bf5bf91442122507b3fdc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18621"/><div sID="gen39372" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18621"/><hi type="bold">2. My brethren--</hi>a phrase often found in James, marking community of nation and of faith.<div eID="gen39372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39373" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all joy--</hi>cause for the highest joy [Grotius]. Nothing but joy [Piscator]. Count all "divers temptations" to be each matter of joy [Bengel].<div eID="gen39373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39374" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fall into--</hi>unexpectedly, so as to be encompassed by them (so the original Greek).<div eID="gen39374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39375" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">temptations--</hi>not in the limited sense of allurements to sin, but trials or distresses of any kind which test and purify the Christian character. Compare "tempt," that is, try, <reference osisRef="Gen.22.1">Ge 22:1</reference>. Some of those to whom James writes were "sick," or otherwise "afflicted" (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.13">Jas 5:13</reference>). Every possible trial to the child of God is a masterpiece of strategy of the Captain of his salvation for his good. <div eID="gen39375" type="x-p"/>
entries.7851c3e6beef83ff128e4f08943be5dd0a5aa287: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18622"/><div sID="gen39376" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18622"/><hi type="bold">3. the trying--</hi>the testing or proving of your faith, namely, by "divers temptations." Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.5.3">Ro 5:3</reference>, tribulation worketh patience, and patience experience (in the original dokime, akin to dokimion, "trying," here; there it is experience: here the "trying" or testing, whence experience flows).<div eID="gen39376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39377" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">patience--</hi>The original implies more; persevering endurance and continuance (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.8.15">Lu 8:15</reference>). <div eID="gen39377" type="x-p"/>
entries.f2a70bcd3e6f3977db7fef34e3343e944e05b7b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18623"/><div sID="gen39378" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18623"/>4. Let endurance have a perfect work (taken out of the previous "worketh patience" or endurance), that is, have its full effect, by showing the most perfect degree of endurance, namely, "joy in bearing the cross" [Menochius], and enduring to the end (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.22">Mt 10:22</reference>) [Calvin].<div eID="gen39378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39379" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye may be perfect--</hi>fully developed in all the attributes of a Christian character. For this there is required "joy" [Bengel], as part of the "perfect work" of probation. The work of God in a man is the man. If God's teachings by patience have had a perfect work in you, you are perfect [Alford].<div eID="gen39379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39380" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">entire--</hi>that which has all its parts complete, wanting no integral part; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.23">1Th 5:23</reference>, "your whole (literally, 'entire') spirit, soul, and body"; as "perfect" implies without a blemish in its parts. <div eID="gen39380" type="x-p"/>
entries.7315866dbf5acec72484515bae2abe27e9f05612: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18624"/><div sID="gen39381" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18624"/>5. English Version omits "But," which the Greek has, and which is important. "But (as this perfect entireness wanting nothing is no easy attainment) if any," &c.<div eID="gen39381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39382" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lack--</hi>rather, as the Greek word is repeated after James's manner, from <reference osisRef="Jas.1.4">Jas 1:4</reference>, "wanting nothing," translate, "If any of you want wisdom," namely, the wisdom whereby ye may "count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations," and "let patience have her perfect work." This "wisdom" is shown in its effects in detail, <reference osisRef="Jas.3.7">Jas 3:7</reference>. The highest wisdom, which governs patience alike in poverty and riches, is described in <reference osisRef="Jas.1.9">Jas 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>.<div eID="gen39382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39383" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ask--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jas.4.2">Jas 4:2</reference>).<div eID="gen39383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39384" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">liberally--</hi>So the Greek is rendered by English Version. It is rendered with simplicity, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.8">Ro 12:8</reference>. God gives without adding aught which may take off from the graciousness of the gift [Alford]. God requires the same "simplicity" in His children ("eye ... single," <reference osisRef="Matt.6.22">Mt 6:22</reference>, literally, "simple").<div eID="gen39384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39385" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upbraideth not--</hi>an illustration of God's giving simply. He gives to the humble suppliant without upbraiding him with his past sin and ingratitude, or his future abuse of God's goodness. The Jews pray, "Let me not have need of the gifts of men, whose gifts are few, but their upbraidings manifold; but give me out of Thy large and full hand." Compare Solomon's prayer for "wisdom," and God's gift above what he asked, though God foresaw his future abuse of His goodness would deserve very differently. James has before his eye the Sermon on the Mount (see my Introduction). God hears every true prayer and grants either the thing asked, or else something better than it; as a good physician consults for his patient's good better by denying something which the latter asks not for his good, than by conceding a temporary gratification to his hurt. <div eID="gen39385" type="x-p"/>
entries.c895038ba0128b2746e0f23dcb35f664c287d8d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18625"/><div sID="gen39386" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18625"/><hi type="bold">6. ask in faith--</hi>that is, the persuasion that God can and will give. James begins and ends with faith. In the middle of the Epistle he removes the hindrances to faith and shows its true character [Bengel].<div eID="gen39386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39387" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wavering--</hi>between belief and unbelief. Compare the case of the Israelites, who seemed to partly believe in God's power, but leaned more to unbelief by "limiting" it. On the other hand, compare <reference osisRef="Acts.10.20">Ac 10:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.4.20">Ro 4:20</reference> ("staggered not ... through unbelief," literally, as here, "wavered not"); <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.8">1Ti 2:8</reference>.<div eID="gen39387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39388" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">like a wave of the sea--</hi><reference osisRef="Isa.57.20">Is 57:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.14">Ep 4:14</reference>, where the same Greek word occurs for "tossed to and fro," as is here translated, "driven with the wind."<div eID="gen39388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39389" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">driven with the wind--</hi>from without.<div eID="gen39389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39390" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tossed--</hi>from within, by its own instability [Bengel]. At one time cast on the shore of faith and hope, at another rolled back into the abyss of unbelief; at one time raised to the height of worldly pride, at another tossed in the sands of despair and affliction [Wiesinger]. <div eID="gen39390" type="x-p"/>
entries.cd7019ac18b5fa3384e8c85804f443fba66200d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18626"/><div sID="gen39391" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18626"/><hi type="bold">7. For--</hi>resumed from "For" in <reference osisRef="Jas.1.6">Jas 1:6</reference>.<div eID="gen39391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39392" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that man--</hi>such a wavering self-deceiver.<div eID="gen39392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39393" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">think--</hi>Real faith is something more than a mere thinking or surmise.<div eID="gen39393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39394" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">anything--</hi>namely, of the things that he prays for: he does receive many things from God, food, raiment, &c., but these are the general gifts of His providence: of the things specially granted in answer to prayer, the waverer shall not receive "anything," much less wisdom. <div eID="gen39394" type="x-p"/>
entries.68660e2bb7042d295cf318f5e535466bfc35145b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18627"/><div sID="gen39395" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18627"/><hi type="bold">8. double-minded--</hi>literally, "double-souled," the one soul directed towards God, the other to something else. The Greek favors Alford's translation, "He (the waverer, <reference osisRef="Jas.1.6">Jas 1:6</reference>) is a man double-minded, unstable," &c.; or better, Beza's. The words in this <reference osisRef="Jas.1.8">Jas 1:8</reference> are in apposition with "that man," <reference osisRef="Jas.1.7">Jas 1:7</reference>; thus the "us," which is not in the original, will not need to be supplied, "A man double-minded, unstable in all his ways!" The word for "double-minded" is found here and in <reference osisRef="Jas.4.8">Jas 4:8</reference>, for the first time in Greek literature. It is not a hypocrite that is meant, but a fickle, "wavering" man, as the context shows. It is opposed to the single eye (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.22">Mt 6:22</reference>). <div eID="gen39395" type="x-p"/>
entries.cd9d7f7c11c9a8721de4d7f363ede480965c7f39: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18628"/><div sID="gen39396" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18628"/>9-10. Translate, "But let the brother," &c. that is, the best remedy against double-mindedness is that Christian simplicity of spirit whereby the "brother," low in outward circumstances, may "rejoice" (answering to <reference osisRef="Jas.1.2">Jas 1:2</reference>) "in that he is exalted," namely, by being accounted a son and heir of God, his very sufferings being a pledge of his coming glory and crown (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.12">Jas 1:12</reference>), and the rich may rejoice "in that he is made low," by being stripped of his goods for Christ's sake [Menochius]; or in that he is made, by sanctified trials, lowly in spirit, which is true matter for rejoicing [Gomarus]. The design of the Epistle is to reduce all things to an equable footing (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.1">Jas 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.13">5:13</reference>). The "low," rather than the "rich," is here called "the brother" [Bengel]. <div eID="gen39396" type="x-p"/>
entries.9defdbeded6464494303df7f36475031e47c6bda: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18630"/><div sID="gen39398" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18630"/>11. Taken from <reference osisRef="Isa.40.6-Isa.40.8">Is 40:6-8</reference>.<div eID="gen39398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39399" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heat--</hi>rather, "the hot wind" from the (east or) south, which scorches vegetation (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.55">Lu 12:55</reference>). The "burning heat" of the sun is not at its rising, but rather at noon; whereas the scorching Kadim wind is often at sunrise (<reference osisRef="Jonah.4.8">Jon 4:8</reference>) [Middleton, The Doctrine of the Greek Article]. <reference osisRef="Matt.20.12">Mt 20:12</reference> uses the Greek word for "heat." <reference osisRef="Isa.40.7">Is 40:7</reference>, "bloweth upon it," seems to answer to "the hot wind" here.<div eID="gen39399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39400" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grace of the fashion--</hi>that is of the external appearance.<div eID="gen39400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39401" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in his ways--</hi>referring to the burdensome extent of the rich man's devices [Bengel]. Compare "his ways," that is, his course of life, <reference osisRef="Jas.1.8">Jas 1:8</reference>. <div eID="gen39401" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7820187e886cea2ef52f74aafea089ed8e4dd83: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18631"/><div sID="gen39402" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18631"/><hi type="bold">12. Blessed--</hi>Compare the beatitudes in the Sermon on the Mount (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.4">Mt 5:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.11">10, 11</reference>).<div eID="gen39402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39403" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">endureth temptation--</hi>not the "falling into divers temptations" (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.2">Jas 1:2</reference>) is the matter for "joy," but the enduring of temptation "unto the end." Compare <reference osisRef="Job.5.17">Job 5:17</reference>.<div eID="gen39403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39404" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when he is tried--</hi>literally, "when he has become tested" or "approved," when he has passed through the "trying" (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.3">Jas 1:3</reference>), his "faith" having finally gained the victory.<div eID="gen39404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39405" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the crown--</hi>not in allusion to the crown or garland given to winners in the games; for this, though a natural allusion for Paul in writing to the heathen, among whom such games existed, would be less appropriate for James in addressing the Jewish Christians, who regarded Gentile usages with aversion.<div eID="gen39405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39406" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of life--</hi>"life" constitutes the crown, literally, the life, the only true life, the highest and eternal life. The crown implies a kingdom (<reference osisRef="Ps.21.3">Psa 21:3</reference>).<div eID="gen39406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39407" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord--</hi>not found in the best manuscripts and versions. The believer's heart fills up the omission, without the name needing to be mentioned. The "faithful One who promised" (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.23">He 10:23</reference>).<div eID="gen39407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39408" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to them that love him--</hi>In <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">2Ti 4:8</reference>, "the crown of righteousness to them that love His appearing." Love produces patient endurance: none attest their love more than they who suffer for Him. <div eID="gen39408" type="x-p"/>
entries.a104aeb4bb121ba7799e7434375a935782fb3c25: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18632"/><div sID="gen39409" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18632"/><hi type="bold">13. when ... tempted--</hi>tried by solicitation to evil. Heretofore the "temptation" meant was that of probation by afflictions. Let no one fancy that God lays upon him an inevitable necessity of sinning. God does not send trials on you in order to make you worse, but to make you better (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.16">Jas 1:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.17">17</reference>). Therefore do not sink under the pressure of evils (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.13">1Co 10:13</reference>).<div eID="gen39409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39410" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of God--</hi>by agency proceeding from God. The Greek is not "tempted by," but, "from," implying indirect agency.<div eID="gen39410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39411" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cannot be tempted with evil, &c.--</hi>"Neither do any of our sins tempt God to entice us to worse things, nor does He tempt any of His own accord" (literally, "of Himself"; compare the antithesis, <reference osisRef="Jas.1.18">Jas 1:18</reference>, "Of His own will He begat us" to holiness, so far is He from tempting us of His own will) [Bengel]. God is said in <reference osisRef="Gen.22.1">Ge 22:1</reference> to have "tempted Abraham"; but there the tempting meant is that of trying or proving, not that of seducement. Alford translates according to the ordinary sense of the Greek, "God is unversed in evil." But as this gives a less likely sense, English Version probably gives the true sense; for ecclesiastical Greek often uses words in new senses, as the exigencies of the new truths to be taught required. <div eID="gen39411" type="x-p"/>
entries.0ff53e31044f2c7ef791f6ea3dcfe55d262a9310: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18633"/><div sID="gen39412" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18633"/>14. Every man, when tempted, is so through being drawn away of (again here, as in <reference osisRef="Jas.1.13">Jas 1:13</reference>, the Greek for "of" expresses the actual source, rather than the agent of temptation) his own lust. The cause of sin is in ourselves. Even Satan's suggestions do not endanger us before they are made our own. Each one has his own peculiar (so the Greek) lust, arising from his own temperament and habit. Lust flows from the original birth-sin in man, inherited from Adam.<div eID="gen39412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39413" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">drawn away--</hi>the beginning step in temptation: drawn away from truth and virtue.<div eID="gen39413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39414" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enticed--</hi>literally, "taken with a bait," as fish are. The further progress: the man allowing himself (as the Greek middle voice implies) to be enticed to evil [Bengel]. "Lust" is here personified as the harlot that allures the man. <div eID="gen39414" type="x-p"/>
entries.3e42dc1fd9e8ad8b9f896bae94464f733f0c510f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18634"/><div sID="gen39415" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18634"/>15. The guilty union is committed by the will embracing the temptress. "Lust," the harlot, then, "brings forth sin," namely, of that kind to which the temptation inclines. Then the particular sin (so the Greek implies), "when it is completed, brings forth death," with which it was all along pregnant [Alford]. This "death" stands in striking contrast to the "crown of life" (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.12">Jas 1:12</reference>) which "patience" or endurance ends in, when it has its "perfect work" (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.4">Jas 1:4</reference>). He who will fight Satan with Satan's own weapons, must not wonder if he finds himself overmatched. Nip sin in the bud of lust. <div eID="gen39415" type="x-p"/>
entries.b8ed5fc57423386711ed7ceabcbd9e634a42e133: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18635"/><div sID="gen39416" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18635"/>16. Do not err in attributing to God temptation to evil; nay (as he proceeds to show), "every good," all that is good on earth, comes from God. <div eID="gen39416" type="x-p"/>
entries.2cf480cc4b88f8e15572cfcb4858bd6ca2748260: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18636"/><div sID="gen39417" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18636"/><hi type="bold">17. gift ... gift--</hi>not the same words in Greek: the first, the act of giving, or the gift in its initiatory stage; the second, the thing given, the boon, when perfected. As the "good gift" stands in contrast to "sin" in its initiatory stage (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.15">Jas 1:15</reference>), so the "perfect boon" is in contrast to "sin when it is finished," bringing forth death (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.3">2Pe 1:3</reference>).<div eID="gen39417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39418" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from above--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Jas.3.15">Jas 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen39418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39419" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Father of lights--</hi>Creator of the lights in heaven (compare <reference osisRef="Job.38.28">Job 38:28</reference> [Alford]; <reference osisRef="Gen.4.20">Ge 4:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.9">He 12:9</reference>). This accords with the reference to the changes in the light of the heavenly bodies alluded to in the end of the verse. Also, Father of the spiritual lights in the kingdom of grace and glory [Bengel]. These were typified by the supernatural lights on the breastplate of the high priest, the Urim. As "God is light, and in Him is no darkness at all" (<reference osisRef="1John.1.5">1Jo 1:5</reference>), He cannot in any way be the Author of sin (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.13">Jas 1:13</reference>), which is darkness (<reference osisRef="John.3.19">Joh 3:19</reference>).<div eID="gen39419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39420" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no variableness ... shadow of turning--</hi>(Mal 3:6). None of the alternations of light and shadow which the physical "lights" undergo, and which even the spiritual lights are liable to, as compared with God. "Shadow of turning," literally, the dark "shadow-mark" cast from one of the heavenly bodies, arising from its "turning" or revolution, for example, when the moon is eclipsed by the shadow of the earth, and the sun by the body of the moon. Bengel makes a climax, "no variation--not even the shadow of a turning"; the former denoting a change in the understanding; the latter, in the will. <div eID="gen39420" type="x-p"/>
entries.c784939e4052bf46de28fae9a9ea1623b14e45ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18637"/><div sID="gen39421" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18637"/>18. (<reference osisRef="John.1.13">Joh 1:13</reference>). The believer's regeneration is the highest example of nothing but good proceeding from God.<div eID="gen39421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39422" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Of his own will--</hi>Of his own good pleasure (which shows that it is God's essential nature to do good, not evil), not induced by any external cause.<div eID="gen39422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39423" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">begat he us--</hi>spiritually: a once-for-all accomplished act (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.3">1Pe 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.23">23</reference>). In contrast to "lust when it hath conceived, bringeth forth sin, and sin ... death" (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.15">Jas 1:15</reference>). Life follows naturally in connection with light (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.17">Jas 1:17</reference>).<div eID="gen39423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39424" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">word of truth--</hi>the Gospel. The objective mean, as faith is the appropriating mean of regeneration by the Holy Spirit as the efficient agent.<div eID="gen39424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39425" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a kind of first-fruits--</hi>Christ is, in respect to the resurrection, "the first-fruits" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.20">1Co 15:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.23">23</reference>): believers, in respect to regeneration, are, as it were, first-fruits (image from the consecration of the first-born of man, cattle, and fruits to God; familiar to the Jews addressed), that is, they are the first of God's regenerated creatures, and the pledge of the ultimate regeneration of the creation, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.19">Ro 8:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.23">23</reference>, where also the Spirit, the divine agent of the believer's regeneration, is termed "the first-fruits," that is, the earnest that the regeneration now begun in the soul, shall at last extend to the body too, and to the lower parts of creation. Of all God's visible creatures, believers are the noblest part, and like the legal "first-fruits," sanctify the rest; for this reason they are much tried now. <div eID="gen39425" type="x-p"/>
entries.301f24e7a1c41ed19de546adc8bef5c7f9dd7732: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18638"/><div sID="gen39426" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18638"/><hi type="bold">19. Wherefore--</hi>as your evil is of yourselves, but your good from God. However, the oldest manuscripts and versions read thus: "Ye know it (so <reference osisRef="Eph.5.5">Ep 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.17">He 12:17</reference>), my beloved brethren; BUT (consequently) let every man be swift to hear," that is, docile in receiving "the word of truth" (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.18">Jas 1:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.21">21</reference>). The true method of hearing is treated in <reference osisRef="Jas.1.21-Jas.1.27">Jas 1:21-27</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jas.2.1-Jas.2.26">Jas 2:1-26</reference>.<div eID="gen39426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39427" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">slow to speak--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.10.19">Pr 10:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.17.27">17:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.17.28">28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.2">Ec 5:2</reference>). A good way of escaping one kind of temptation arising from ourselves (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.13">Jas 1:13</reference>). Slow to speak authoritatively as a master or teacher of others (compare <reference osisRef="Jas.3.1">Jas 3:1</reference>): a common Jewish fault: slow also to speak such hasty things of God, as in <reference osisRef="Jas.1.13">Jas 1:13</reference>. Two ears are given to us, the rabbis observe, but only one tongue: the ears are open and exposed, whereas the tongue is walled in behind the teeth.<div eID="gen39427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39428" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">slow to wrath--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jas.3.13">Jas 3:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jas.3.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.5">4:5</reference>). Slow in becoming heated by debate: another Jewish fault (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.8">Ro 2:8</reference>), to which much speaking tends. Tittmann thinks not so much "wrath" is meant, as an indignant feeling of fretfulness under the calamities to which the whole of human life is exposed; this accords with the "divers temptations" in <reference osisRef="Jas.1.2">Jas 1:2</reference>. Hastiness of temper hinders hearing God's word; so Naaman, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.11">2Ki 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.4.28">Lu 4:28</reference>. <div eID="gen39428" type="x-p"/>
entries.b78605fe4f78191b7d21f79f0f8317448de4d549: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18639"/><div sID="gen39429" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18639"/>20. Man's angry zeal in debating, as if jealous for the honor of God's righteousness, is far from working that which is really righteousness in God's sight. True "righteousness is sown in peace," not in wrath (<reference osisRef="Jas.3.18">Jas 3:18</reference>). The oldest and best reading means "worketh," that is, practiceth not: the received reading is "worketh," produceth not. <div eID="gen39429" type="x-p"/>
entries.226097471b892b70b30d9fec7a564b40b4ffa880: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18640"/><div sID="gen39430" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18640"/><hi type="bold">21. lay apart--</hi>"once for all" (so the Greek): as a filthy garment. Compare Joshua's filthy garments, <reference osisRef="Zech.3.3">Zec 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.3.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.14">Re 7:14</reference>. "Filthiness" is cleansed away by hearing the word (<reference osisRef="John.15.3">Joh 15:3</reference>).<div eID="gen39430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39431" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">superfluity of naughtiness--</hi>excess (for instance, the intemperate spirit implied in "wrath," <reference osisRef="Jas.1.19">Jas 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">20</reference>), which arises from malice (our natural, evil disposition towards one another). <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.1">1Pe 2:1</reference> has the very same words in the Greek. So "malice" is the translation, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.31">Ep 4:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.8">Col 3:8</reference>. "Faulty excess" [Bengel] is not strong enough. Superfluous excess in speaking is also reprobated as "coming of evil" (the Greek is akin to the word for "naughtiness" here) in the Sermon on the Mount (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.37">Mt 5:37</reference>), with which James' Epistle is so connected.<div eID="gen39431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39432" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with meekness--</hi>in mildness towards one another [Alford], the opposite to "wrath" (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.20">Jas 1:20</reference>): answering to "as new-born babes" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.2">1Pe 2:2</reference>). Meekness, I think, includes also a childlike, docile, humble, as well as an uncontentious, spirit (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.9">Psa 25:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.45.4">45:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.2">Is 66:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.5.5">Mt 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.11.28-Matt.11.30">11:28-30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.18.3">18:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.18.4">4</reference>; contrast <reference osisRef="Rom.2.8">Ro 2:8</reference>). On "receive," applied to ground receiving seed, compare <reference osisRef="Mark.4.20">Mr 4:20</reference>. Contrast <reference osisRef="Acts.17.11">Ac 17:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.6">1Th 1:6</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.10">2Th 2:10</reference>.<div eID="gen39432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39433" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">engrafted word--</hi>the Gospel word, whose proper attribute is to be engrafted by the Holy Spirit, so as to be livingly incorporated with the believer, as the fruitful shoot is with the wild natural stock on which it is engrafted. The law came to man only from without, and admonished him of his duty. The Gospel is engrafted inwardly, and so fulfils the ultimate design of the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.6.6">De 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.18">11:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.11">Psa 119:11</reference>). Alford translates, "The implanted word," referring to the parable of the sower (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.1-Matt.13.23">Mt 13:1-23</reference>). I prefer English Version.<div eID="gen39433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39434" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">able to save--</hi>a strong incentive to correct our dulness in hearing the word: that word which we hear so carelessly, is able (instrumentally) to save us [Calvin].<div eID="gen39434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39435" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">souls--</hi>your true selves, for the "body" is now liable to sickness and death: but the soul being now saved, both soul and body at last shall be so (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.15">Jas 5:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jas.5.20">20</reference>). <div eID="gen39435" type="x-p"/>
entries.f8c9604e653afc1f8685e45cb9ff1627131bdf59: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18641"/><div sID="gen39436" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18641"/>22. Qualification of the precept, "Be swift to hear": "Be ye doers ... not hearers only"; not merely "Do the word," but "Be doers" systematically and continually, as if this was your regular business. James here again refers to the Sermon on the Mount (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.21-Matt.7.29">Mt 7:21-29</reference>).<div eID="gen39436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39437" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deceiving your own selves--</hi>by the logical fallacy (the Greek implies this) that the mere hearing is all that is needed. <div eID="gen39437" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa5eaa40bdf263e506c02aad1ce181c91b989421: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18642"/><div sID="gen39438" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18642"/><hi type="bold">23. For--</hi>the logical self-deceit (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.22">Jas 1:22</reference>) illustrated.<div eID="gen39438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39439" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not a doer--</hi>more literally, "a notdoer" [Alford]. The true disciple, say the rabbis, learns in order that he may do, not in order that he may merely know or teach.<div eID="gen39439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39440" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his natural face--</hi>literally, "the countenance of his birth": the face he was born with. As a man may behold his natural face in a mirror, so the hearer may perceive his moral visage in God's Word. This faithful portraiture of man's soul in Scripture, is the strongest proof of the truth of the latter. In it, too, we see mirrored God's glory, as well as our natural vileness. <div eID="gen39440" type="x-p"/>
entries.e2399dce394ad37bb565e9d8e7cb025d1dec46e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18643"/><div sID="gen39441" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18643"/><hi type="bold">24. beholdeth--</hi>more literally, "he contemplated himself and hath gone his way," that is, no sooner has he contemplated his image than he is gone his way (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.11">Jas 1:11</reference>). "Contemplate" answers to hearing the word: <hi type="bold">"goeth his way," to relaxing the attention after hearing--</hi>letting the mind go elsewhere, and the interest of the thing heard pass away: then forgetfulness follows [Alford] (Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.31">Eze 33:31</reference>). "Contemplate" here, and in <reference osisRef="Jas.1.23">Jas 1:23</reference>, implies that, though cursory, yet some knowledge of one's self, at least for the time, is imparted in hearing the word (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.24">1Co 14:24</reference>).<div eID="gen39441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39442" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and ... and--</hi>The repetition expresses hastiness joined with levity [Bengel].<div eID="gen39442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39443" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forgetteth what manner of man he was--</hi>in the mirror. Forgetfulness is no excuse (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.25">Jas 1:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.9">2Pe 1:9</reference>). <div eID="gen39443" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe51c8490fd3d0e6d4cef6191139346bc2df406b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18644"/><div sID="gen39444" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18644"/><hi type="bold">25. looketh into--</hi>literally, "stoopeth down to take a close look into." Peers into: stronger than "beholdeth," or "contemplated," <reference osisRef="Jas.1.24">Jas 1:24</reference>. A blessed curiosity if it be efficacious in bearing fruit [Bengel].<div eID="gen39444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39445" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perfect law of liberty--</hi>the Gospel rule of life, perfect and perfecting (as shown in the Sermon on the Mount, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.48">Mt 5:48</reference>), and making us truly walk at liberty (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.32">Psa 119:32</reference>, Church of England Prayer Book Version). Christians are to aim at a higher standard of holiness than was generally understood under the law. The principle of love takes the place of the letter of the law, so that by the Spirit they are free from the yoke of sin, and free to obey by spontaneous instinct (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.8">Jas 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.12">10, 12</reference>; Joh 8:31-36; 15:<reference osisRef="John.14.15">14, 15</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.22">1Co 7:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.1">Ga 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.16">1Pe 2:16</reference>). The law is thus not made void, but fulfilled.<div eID="gen39445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39446" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">continueth therein--</hi>contrasted with "goeth his way," <reference osisRef="Jas.1.24">Jas 1:24</reference>, continues both looking into the mirror of God's word, and doing its precepts.<div eID="gen39446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39447" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doer of the work--</hi>rather, "a doer of work" [Alford], an actual worker.<div eID="gen39447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39448" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blessed in his deed--</hi>rather, "in his doing"; in the very doing there is blessedness (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.11">Psa 19:11</reference>). <div eID="gen39448" type="x-p"/>
entries.cdebbdee43a17f1f2b2af7443f158b8dd6250a5d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18645"/><div sID="gen39449" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18645"/>26-27. An example of doing work.<div eID="gen39449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39450" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">religious ... religion--</hi>The Greek expresses the external service or exercise of religion, "godliness" being the internal soul of it. "If any man think himself to be (so the Greek) religious, that is, observant of the offices of religion, let him know these consist not so much in outward observances, as in such acts of mercy and humble piety (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.7">Mi 6:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.8">8</reference>) as visiting the fatherless, &c., and keeping one's self unspotted from the world" (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.23">Mt 23:23</reference>). James does not mean that these offices are the great essentials, or sum total of religion; but that, whereas the law service was merely ceremonial, the very services of the Gospel consist in acts of mercy and holiness, and it has light for its garment, its very robe being righteousness [Trench]. The Greek word is only found in <reference osisRef="Acts.26.5">Ac 26:5</reference>, "after the straitest sect of our religion I lived a Pharisee." <reference osisRef="Col.2.18">Col 2:18</reference>, "worshipping of angels."<div eID="gen39450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39451" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bridleth not ... tongue--</hi>Discretion in speech is better than fluency of speech (compare <reference osisRef="Jas.3.2">Jas 3:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jas.3.3">3</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.39.1">Psa 39:1</reference>. God alone can enable us to do so. James, in treating of the law, naturally notices this sin. For they who are free from grosser sins, and even bear the outward show of sanctity, will often exalt themselves by detracting others under the pretense of zeal, while their real motive is love of evil-speaking [Calvin].<div eID="gen39451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39452" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heart--</hi>It and the tongue act and react on one another. <div eID="gen39452" type="x-p"/>

entries.54f24243438a2936e37fa72806e71b142682d9eb: <div eID="gen53908" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Preface to the General Epistle of James</title> <div sID="gen53909" type="x-p"/> There have been more doubts, and more diversity of opinion, concerning the author of this epistle, and the time in which it was written, than about most other parts of the New Testament. To enter at large into a discussion of the opinions of ancient and modern writers on this subject would tend but little to the establishment of truth, or to the edification of the reader. <div eID="gen53909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53910" type="x-p"/> Lardner, Michaelis, and Macknight, have entered considerably into the controversy relative to the author, the time, and the canonical authority of this book; and to them the reader who wishes to see the difficulties with which the subject is pressed may have recourse. <div eID="gen53910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53911" type="x-p"/> This epistle, with those of Peter, John, and Jude, is termed catholic, καθολικη , from κατα, through, and ὁλος, the whole; for the application of which term Ecumenius, in cap. i. Jacobi, gives the following reason: Καθολικαι λεγονται αυται, οἱονει εγκυκλιοι· ου γαρ αφωρισμενως εθνει ἑνι η πολει, αλλα καθολου τοις πιστοις· "These epistles are called catholic, universal, or circular, because they were not written to one nation or city, but to believers everywhere." <div eID="gen53911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53912" type="x-p"/> Yet, as these epistles had some difficulty at first to get into general circulation, but at last were everywhere received, it is more likely that they obtained the term catholic from the circumstance of their being at last universally acknowledged as canonical; so that the word catholic is to be understood here in the same sense as canonical. <div eID="gen53912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53913" type="x-p"/> Who the writer of the epistle in question was, is difficult to say; all that we know certainly is, from his own words, that his name was James, and that he was a servant of God, and of the Lord Jesus. Two persons of this name are mentioned in the New Testament; James the son of Zebedee, called also James the elder; and James του μικρου, the less or the little one, called the son of Alpheus, and brother of our Lord: but whether one of these, or if one of them, which, or whether one of the same name different from both, are points that cannot be satisfactorily determined. Michaelis, who has examined the subject with his usual ability, leaves the matter in doubt; but leans to the opinion that James the son of Zebedee was the author, and that this epistle was written before any of those in the New Testament. Other great authorities ascribe it to James, called the brother of our Lord, who was president, or bishop, of the Church in Jerusalem. Even allowing this opinion to be correct, it is not agreed in what sense James is called our Lord's brother, there being four or five different opinions concerning the meaning of this term. From <reference osisRef="Mat.13.55">Mat 13:55</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.56">Mat 13:56</reference>, we learn that there were four persons called brethren of our Lord: "Is not this the carpenter's son? Is not his mother called Mary? And his brethren James, and Joses, and Simon, and Judas? And his sisters, are they not all with us?" Now, it is generally allowed that the James here is the author of this epistle, and the Jude or Judas, mentioned with him, the author of that which stands last in this collection. But with respect to the meaning of the term brother, as here used, it will be necessary to state the opinions of learned men: - <div eID="gen53913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53914" type="x-p"/> 1. It is supposed that these were children of Joseph, by a former marriage; this is a very ancient opinion; as there is nothing improbable in the supposition that Joseph was a widower when he married the blessed virgin. <div eID="gen53914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53915" type="x-p"/> 2. They are supposed to have been children of Joseph and his wife Mary; all born after the birth of our Lord. This is an opinion extremely probable: see some reasons for it in the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.13.55">Mat 13:55</reference> (note); see also on <reference osisRef="Mat.1.25">Mat 1:25</reference> (note). <div eID="gen53915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53916" type="x-p"/> 3. That they were called our Lord's brethren, because children of Joseph by the wife of one of his brothers, who had died childless, and whose widow Joseph took, according to the Mosaic law, to raise up seed to his deceased brother. This is very unlikely, because, in this case, it would have been only requisite for Joseph to have had one male by his brother's wife; but here we find four, besides several sisters. <div eID="gen53916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53917" type="x-p"/> 4. That Cleophas, called also Alpheus, married a sister of the blessed virgin, called also Mary, by whom he had the above issue; and that these were called brethren of our Lord, from the common custom among the Hebrews, to term all the more immediately cognate branches of the same family, brothers' and sisters' children, i.e. cousins-german, brethren. These, therefore, being aunt's children of our Lord, are, according to this usage, called his brethren. The first and second of these opinions appear to me the most probable; though most modern writers are of the latter opinion. <div eID="gen53917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53918" type="x-p"/> That of the two James's, James the less was the author of this epistle, Dr. Macknight thinks, following Lardner and others, is incontestable: I shall quote his abridgment of Lardner's arguments; but the point in question is not, in my opinion, made out by any of these writers. "In the catalogue of the apostles, <reference osisRef="Mat.10.2">Mat 10:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mar.3.17">Mar 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.6.14">Luk 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.1.13">Act 1:13</reference>; we find two persons of the name of James; the first was the son of Zebedee, <reference osisRef="Mat.10.2">Mat 10:2</reference>; the second in all the catalogues is called the son of Alpheus: one of these apostles is called, <reference osisRef="Gal.1.19">Gal 1:19</reference>, the Lord's brother. Wherefore, as there were only twelve apostles, and as James the son of Zebedee, so far as we know, was in no respect related to our Lord, the apostle called James, the Lord's brother, must have been James the son of Alpheus, called also James the less or younger, whose relation to Christ will appear by comparing <reference osisRef="Mar.15.40">Mar 15:40</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Joh.19.25">Joh 19:25</reference>. In the former passage, Mark, speaking of the women who were present at the crucifixion, says: 'There were also women looking on afar off, among whom were Mary Magdalen, and Mary the mother of James the less and of Joses, and Salome.' In the latter passage, John, speaking of the same women, says: 'There stood by the cross of Jesus, his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary, the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalen:' wherefore, our Lord's mother's sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, mentioned by John, is in all probability the person whom Mark calls Mary the mother of James the less, and of Joses; consequently, her sons, James and Joses, were our Lord's cousins-german by his mother. And as the Hebrews called all near relations brethren, it is more than probable that James the son of Alpheus, who was our Lord's cousin-german, is James the Lord's brother, mentioned <reference osisRef="Gal.1.19">Gal 1:19</reference>. Three circumstances confirm this opinion: <div eID="gen53918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53919" type="x-p"/> 1. James and Joses, the sons of Mary, our Lord's mother's sister, are expressly called the brethren of Jesus, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.55">Mat 13:55</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mar.6.3">Mar 6:3</reference>. <div eID="gen53919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53920" type="x-p"/> 2. James, the son of our Lord's mother's sister, being distinguished from another James by the appellation of the less, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.40">Mar 15:40</reference>, there is good reason to suppose that he is the James whom Mark, in his catalogue, distinguishes from James the son of Zebedee, by the appellation of the son of Alpheus. It is true, Mary the mother of James and of Joses, is called the wife of Cleophas, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.25">Joh 19:25</reference> : but Cleophas and Alpheus are the same name differently pronounced; the one according to the Hebrew, and the other according to the Greek, orthography. <div eID="gen53920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53921" type="x-p"/> 3. Of the persons called the brethren of Jesus, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.55">Mat 13:55</reference>, there are three mentioned in the catalogue as Apostles: James, and Simon, and Judas. They, I suppose, are the brethren of the Lord, who are said, as apostles, to have had a right to lead about a sister or a wife, etc.; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.5">1Cor 9:5</reference>. <div eID="gen53921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53922" type="x-p"/> Jerome likewise thought James the Lord's brother was so called because he was the son of Mary, our Lord's mother's sister; Art. Jacobus. Lardner, Canon., vol. iii. p. 63, says: 'Jerome seems to have been the first who said our Lord's brethren were the sons of his mother's sister; and this opinion was at length embraced by Augustine, and has prevailed very much of late, being the opinion of the Romanists in general, and of Lightfoot, Witsius, Lampe, and many of the Protestants. On the other hand, Origen, Epiphanius, and other ancient writers, both Greeks and Latins, were of opinion that James, the Lord's brother, was not the son of the virgin's sister, but of Joseph, our Lord's reputed father, by a former wife, who died before he espoused the virgin. Of the same opinion were Vossius, Basnage, and Cave, among the Protestants; and Valesius among the Romanists. Epiphanius and Theophylact supposed that Joseph's first wife was the widow of Alpheus, who, being Joseph's brother, Joseph married her to raise up seed to him; and therefore James, the issue of that marriage, was fitly called the won of Alpheus, and brother of our Lord.' But these suppositions might have been spared, if the ancients and moderns had recollected that near relations were called brethren by the Hebrews, and that Alpheus and Cleophas are the same names differently written; James the less, the son of Alpheus, being not only the Lord's near relation, but an apostle, whom, as is generally supposed, he honored in a particular manner, by appearing to him alone, after his resurrection; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.7">1Cor 15:7</reference>. These circumstances, together with his own personal merit, rendered him of such note among the apostles that they appointed him to reside at Jerusalem, and to superintend the Church there. This appointment, Lardner says, was made soon after the martyrdom of Stephen; and, in support of this opinion, observes, 'that Peter always speaks first, as president among the apostles, until after the choice of the seven deacons. Every thing said of St. James, after that, implies his presiding in the Church at Jerusalem.' Canon., vol. iii. p. 28. For example, when the apostles and elders at Jerusalem came together to consider whether it was needful to circumcise the Gentiles, after there had been much disputing, Peter spake, <reference osisRef="Act.15.7">Act 15:7</reference>, then Barnabas and Paul, <reference osisRef="Act.15.12">Act 15:12</reference>. And when they had ended, James summed up the whole, and proposed the terms on which the Gentiles were to be received into the Church, <reference osisRef="Act.15.19-Act.15.21">Act 15:19-21</reference>; to which the whole assembly agreed, and wrote letters to the Gentiles, conformably to the opinion of James, <reference osisRef="Act.15.22-Act.15.29">Act 15:22-29</reference>. From this it is inferred, that James presided in the council of Jerusalem, because he was president of the Church in that city. "Chrysostom, in his Homily on Acts 15, says: 'James was bishop of Jerusalem, and therefore spoke last:' In the time of this council, Paul communicated the Gospel which he preached among the Gentiles to three of the apostles, whom he calls pillars; and tells us that, when they perceived the inspiration and miraculous powers which he possessed, they gave him the right hand of fellowship, mentioning James first, <reference osisRef="Gal.2.9">Gal 2:9</reference> : 'And knowing the grace that was bestowed on me, James, Cephas, and John, who were pillars, gave to me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship.' This implies that James, whom, in the first chapter, he had called the Lord's brother, was not only an apostle, but the presiding apostle in the Church at Jerusalem. In the same chapter, Paul, giving an account of what happened after the council, says, <reference osisRef="Gal.2.11">Gal 2:11</reference> : 'When Peter was come to Antioch, before that certain came from James, he did eat with the Gentiles; but when they were come he withdrew, and separated himself, fearing them who were of the circumcision.' This shows that James resided at Jerusalem, and presided in the Church there, and was greatly respected by the Jewish believers. The same circumstance appears from <reference osisRef="Act.21.17">Act 21:17</reference>, where, giving an account of Paul's journey to Jerusalem, with the collections from the saints in Judea, Luke says, <reference osisRef="Act.21.18">Act 21:18</reference> : 'Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present.' Farther, the respect in which James was held by the apostles appears from two facts recorded by Luke: the first is, when Paul came to Jerusalem, three years after his conversion, Barnabas took him, and brought him Peter and James, as the chief apostles. Compare <reference osisRef="Act.9.27">Act 9:27</reference> with <reference osisRef="Gal.1.19">Gal 1:19</reference>. The second fact is, after Peter was miraculously delivered out of prison, about the time of the passover, in the year 44, 'he came to the house of Mary - where many were gathered together praying; (<reference osisRef="Act.12.12">Act 12:12</reference>); and when he had declared to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison, he said, Go, show these things to James, and to the brethren;' <reference osisRef="Act.12.17">Act 12:17</reference>. These particulars are mentioned by Lardner, and before him by Whitby and Cave, to show that James, the Lord's brother, was really an apostle, in the strict acceptation of the word; consequently, that Eusebius was mistaken when he placed him among the seventy disciples; E. H., lib. vii. c. 12. "That the Epistle of James was early esteemed an inspired writing, is evident from the following fact: that while the Second Epistle of Peter, the second and third of John, the Epistle of Jude, and the Revelation, are omitted in the first Syriac translation of the New Testament, (the Peshito), which was made in the beginning of the second century for the use of the converted Jews; the Epistle of James has found a place in it, equally with the books which were never called in question. This is an argument of great weight; for certainly the Jewish believers, to whom that epistle was addressed and delivered, were much better judges of its authenticity than the converted Gentiles, to whom it was not sent, and who perhaps had no opportunity of being acquainted with it till long after it was written. Wherefore its being received by the Jewish believers is an undeniable proof that they knew it to be written by James the apostle; whereas the ignorance of the Gentile believers, concerning this epistle, is not even a presumption against its authenticity. "That the converted Gentiles had little knowledge of the Epistle of James in the first ages, may have been owing to various causes; such as, that it was addressed to the Jews, and that the matters contained in it were personal to the Jews. For on these accounts the Jewish believers may have thought it not necessary to communicate it to the Gentiles. And when it was made known to them, they may have scrupled to receive it as an inspired writing for the following reasons: <div eID="gen53922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53923" type="x-p"/> 1. The writer does not, in the inscription, take the title of an apostle, but calls himself simply James, a servant of God, and of the Lord Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen53923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53924" type="x-p"/> 2. Many of the ancients, by calling the writer of this epistle James the Just, have rendered his apostleship doubtful. <div eID="gen53924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53925" type="x-p"/> 3. As they have done, likewise, by speaking of him commonly as bishop of Jerusalem, and not as an apostle of Christ. <div eID="gen53925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53926" type="x-p"/> It is little wonder, therefore, that this epistle was not received generally by the converted Gentiles; consequently that it was not often quoted by them in their writings. But afterwards, when it was considered that this epistle was from the beginning received by the Jewish believers, and that it was translated into the Syriac language for their use; and that Paul, though an apostle, sometimes contented himself with the appellation of a servant of Christ, <reference osisRef="Phi.1.1">Phi 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Plm.1.1">Plm 1:1</reference>; and sometimes took no appellation but his own name; <reference osisRef="1Thes.1.1">1Thes 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thes.1.1">2Thes 1:1</reference>; and that the apostle John did not, in any of his epistles, call himself an apostle; the title which the author of the Epistle of James had to be an apostle was no longer doubted, but he was generally acknowledged to be James, the son of Alpheus, and the Lord's brother; and his epistle, after an accurate examination, was received as an inspired writing. So Estius tells us, who affirms that after the fourth century no Church nor ecclesiastical writer is found who ever doubted of the authority of this epistle; but, on the contrary; all the catalogues of the books of Scripture published, whether by general or provincial councils, or by Roman bishops, or other orthodox writers, since the fourth century, constantly number it among the canonical Scriptures. "With respect to what is remarked by Eusebius, that there are not many ancient writers who have quoted the Epistle of James, learned men have observed that Clement of Rome has quoted it four several times; and so does Ignatius in his genuine Epistle to the Ephesians, sec. 10, 12, 17, 30; and Origen in his thirteenth Homily on Genesis, sec. 5. That it was not more generally quoted by the ancients, besides the things already mentioned, may have been owing to the following reasons: <div eID="gen53926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53927" type="x-p"/> 1. Being written to the whole Jewish nation to correct the errors and vices which prevailed among them, the Gentiles may have thought themselves little concerned with it, and may have been at no pains to procure copies of it; by which means it was not so generally known among them as some other books of Scripture. <div eID="gen53927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53928" type="x-p"/> 2. The seeming opposition of the doctrine of this epistle to the doctrine of Paul, concerning justification by faith without the works of the law, may have occasioned it to be less regarded by the most ancient writers; just as it was in later times, on the same account, rejected by Luther, who, to show his contempt of it, called it (epistola straminea) a strawy or chaffy epistle. "To conclude, the authority of the Epistle of James, as an inspired writing, is abundantly established, in Mill's opinion, by the Apostles Paul and Peter, who have in their writings many sentiments and expressions similar to those contained in this epistle; for example: - <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.3">1Pet 1:3</reference> : Who hath begotten us again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. <reference osisRef="Jam.1.18">Jam 1:18</reference> : Having willed it, he hath begotten us by the word. <reference osisRef="Rom.5.3">Rom 5:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.4">Rom 5:4</reference> : Knowing that affliction worketh out patience; and patience experience. <reference osisRef="Jam.1.3">Jam 1:3</reference> : Knowing that the proving of your faith worketh out patience. <reference osisRef="Rom.2.13">Rom 2:13</reference> : That the hearers of the law are not just before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified. <reference osisRef="Jam.1.22">Jam 1:22</reference> : And be ye doers of the law, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves by false reasoning. <reference osisRef="Rom.7.23">Rom 7:23</reference> : I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind. <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.11">1Pet 2:11</reference> : Lusts which war against the soul. <reference osisRef="Jam.4.1">Jam 4:1</reference> : Come they not hence, even from your lusts, which war in your members? <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.8">1Pet 5:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.9">1Pet 5:9</reference> : Your adversary the devil; whom resist, steadfast in the faith. <reference osisRef="Jam.4.7">Jam 4:7</reference> : Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.6">1Pet 5:6</reference> : Be humbled under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you. <reference osisRef="Jam.4.10">Jam 4:10</reference> : Be humbled in the presence of God, and he will lift you up. <reference osisRef="Rom.14.4">Rom 14:4</reference> : Who art thou that condemnest another man's household servant? <reference osisRef="Jam.4.12">Jam 4:12</reference> : Thou, who art thou that condemnest another? <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.8">1Pet 4:8</reference> : Love covereth a multitude of sins. <reference osisRef="Jam.5.20">Jam 5:20</reference> : Will cover a multitude of sins." <div eID="gen53928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53929" type="x-p"/> See Macknight's preface. <div eID="gen53929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53930" type="x-p"/> That James the less may have been our Lord's cousin-german, or even our Lord's brother by a former wife of Joseph, or even by the virgin, is perfectly possible; and that he was an apostle, and an eminent man among both Jews and Christians, may be readily credited; and that he was author of this epistle, is also possible: but I must still assert that we have neither decisive nor satisfactory evidence on this subject; and that it is arguing in a circle to deduce the evidence of its authenticity from the apostleship of James the less, because this person is not proved to be its author. The chief and proper evidence of its being canonical must be taken from the fact that it was universally received by the Church of Christ, and without scruple incorporated with those writings, which were, on all hands, allowed to have been given by the inspiration of God. <div eID="gen53930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53931" type="x-p"/> Before I conclude, I shall mention the opinion of Michaelis relative to the author of this epistle. "All things considered," says he, "I see no ground for the assertion that James, the son of Zebedee, was not the author of this epistle. One circumstance affords, at least, a presumptive argument in favor of the opinion that it was really written by the elder James, and at a time when the Gospel had not been propagated among the Gentiles; namely, that it contains no exhortations to harmony between the Jewish and Gentile converts, which, after the time that the Gentiles were admitted into the Church, became absolutely necessary. Had it been written after the apostolic council of Jerusalem, mentioned Acts 15, and by the younger James, we might have expected that, at least, some allusion would be made in it to the decree of that council, which was propounded by the younger James in favor of the Gentile converts; and that the epistle would contain an admonition to the Jewish converts, to consider the Gentile converts as their brethren." - Introduction to the New Testament. <div eID="gen53931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53932" type="x-p"/> The epistle itself is entirely different in its complexion from all those in the sacred canon; the style and manner are more that of a Jewish prophet than a Christian apostle. It scarcely touches on any subject purely Christian. Our blessed Lord is only mentioned twice in it, <reference osisRef="Jam.1.1">Jam 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jam.2.1">Jam 2:1</reference>; but it has nothing of his miracles or teaching, of his death or resurrection, nor of any redemption by him. It begins without any apostolical salutation, and ends without any apostolical benediction. In short, had it not been for the two slight notices of our blessed Lord, we had not known it was the work of any Christian writer. It may be considered a sort of connecting link between Judaism and Christianity, as the ministry of John Baptist was between the old covenant and the new. There is neither plan nor arrangement in it; but it contains many invaluable lessons which no serious person can read without profit. <div eID="gen53932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53933" type="x-p"/> James the less was martyred at Jerusalem about a.d. 62: and the epistle is supposed to have been written a short time before his death. Though I believe it to be the work of an unknown author, not long after the ascension of our Lord, I shall follow the usual chronology, and date it in the year 61; not because I think that to be the true date, but because it is what is generally adopted. <div eID="gen53933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53934" type="x-p"/> He addresses the dispersed of the twelve tribes, <reference osisRef="Jam.1.1">Jam 1:1</reference>. Shows that they should rejoice under the cross, because of the spiritual good which they may derive from it, especially in the increase and perfecting of their patience, <reference osisRef="Jam.1.2-Jam.1.4">Jam 1:2-4</reference>. They are exhorted to ask wisdom of God, who gives liberally to all, <reference osisRef="Jam.1.5">Jam 1:5</reference>. But they must ask in faith, and not with a doubting mind, <reference osisRef="Jam.1.6-Jam.1.8">Jam 1:6-8</reference>. Directions to the rich and the poor, <reference osisRef="Jam.1.9-Jam.1.11">Jam 1:9-11</reference>. The blessedness of the man that endures trials, <reference osisRef="Jam.1.12">Jam 1:12</reference>. How men are tempted and drawn away from God, <reference osisRef="Jam.1.13-Jam.1.15">Jam 1:13-15</reference>. God is the Father of lights, and all good proceeds from him, <reference osisRef="Jam.1.16-Jam.1.18">Jam 1:16-18</reference>. Cautions against hasty words and wrong tempers, <reference osisRef="Jam.1.19-Jam.1.21">Jam 1:19-21</reference>. We should be doers of the word, and not hearers merely, lest we resemble those who, beholding their natural face in a glass, when it is removed forget what manner of persons they were, <reference osisRef="Jam.1.22-Jam.1.24">Jam 1:22-24</reference>. We should look into the perfect law of liberty, and continue therein, <reference osisRef="Jam.1.25">Jam 1:25</reference>. The nature and properties of pure religion, <reference osisRef="Jam.1.26">Jam 1:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jam.1.27">Jam 1:27</reference>. <div eID="gen53934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53935" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen53935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53936" type="x-p"/> James, a servant of God - For an account of this person, or rather for the conjectures concerning him, see the preface. He neither calls himself an apostle, nor does he say that he was the brother of Christ, or bishop of Jerusalem; whether he was James the elder, son of Zebedee, or James the less, called our Lord's brother, or some other person of the same name, we know not. The assertions of writers concerning these points are worthy of no regard. The Church has always received him as an apostle of Christ. <div eID="gen53936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53937" type="x-p"/> To the twelve tribes - scattered abroad - To the Jews, whether converted to Christianity or not, who lived out of Judea, and sojourned among the Gentiles for the purpose of trade or commerce. At this time there were Jews partly traveling, partly sojourning, and partly resident in most parts of the civilized world; particularly in Asia, Greece, Egypt, and Italy. I see no reason for restricting it to Jewish believers only; it was sent to all whom it might concern, but particularly to those who had received the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ; much less must we confine it to those who were scattered abroad at the persecution raised concerning Stephen, <reference osisRef="Act.8.1">Act 8:1</reference>, etc.; <reference osisRef="Act.11.19">Act 11:19</reference>, etc. That the twelve tribes were in actual existence when James wrote this epistle, Dr. Macknight thinks evident from the following facts: "1. Notwithstanding Cyrus allowed all the Jews in his dominions to return to their own land, many of them did not return. This happened agreeably to God's purpose, in permitting them to be carried captive into Assyria and Babylonia; for he intended to make himself known among the heathens, by means of the knowledge of his being and perfections, which the Jews, in their dispersion, would communicate to them. This also was the reason that God determined that the ten tribes should never return to their own land, <reference osisRef="Hos.1.6">Hos 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.8">Hos 8:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.9.3">Hos 9:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.9.15-Hos.9.17">Hos 9:15-17</reference>. <div eID="gen53937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53938" type="x-p"/> 2. That, comparatively speaking, few of the twelve tribes returned in consequence of Cyrus's decree, but continued to live among the Gentiles, appears from this: that in the days of Ahasuerus, one of the successors of Cyrus, who reigned from India to Ethiopia, over one hundred and twenty-seven provinces, <reference osisRef="Est.3.8">Est 3:8</reference>, The Jews were dispersed among the people in all the provinces of his kingdom, and their laws were diverse from the laws of all other people, and they did not keep the king's laws; so that, by adhering to their own usages, they kept themselves distinct from all the nations among whom they lived. <div eID="gen53938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53939" type="x-p"/> 3. On the day of pentecost, which happened next after our Lord's ascension, <reference osisRef="Act.2.5">Act 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.2.9">Act 2:9</reference>, There were dwelling at Jerusalem Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven; Parthians, Medes, and Elamites, etc.; so numerous were the Jews, and so widely dispersed through all the countries of the world. <div eID="gen53939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53940" type="x-p"/> 4. When Paul traveled through Asia and Europe, he found the Jews so numerous, that in all the noted cities of the Gentiles they had synagogues in which they assembled for the worship of God, and were joined by multitudes of proselytes from among the heathens, to whom likewise he preached the Gospel. <div eID="gen53940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53941" type="x-p"/> 5. The same apostle, in his speech to King Agrippa, affirmed that the twelve tribes were then existing, and that they served God day and night, in expectation of the promise made to the fathers, <reference osisRef="Act.26.6">Act 26:6</reference>. <div eID="gen53941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53942" type="x-p"/> 6. Josephus, Ant. i. 14, cap. 12, tells us that one region could not contain the Jews, but they dwelt in most of the flourishing cities of Asia and Europe, in the islands and continent, not much less in number than the heathen inhabitants. From all this it is evident that the Jews of the dispersion were more numerous than even the Jews in Judea, and that James very properly inscribed this letter to the twelve tribes which were in the dispersion, seeing the twelve tribes really existed then, and do still exist, although not distinguished by separate habitations, as they were anciently in their own land. <div eID="gen53942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53943" type="x-p"/> Greeting - Χαιρειν· Health; a mere expression of benevolence, a wish for their prosperity; a common form of salutation; see <reference osisRef="Act.15.23">Act 15:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.23.26">Act 23:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Jn.1.11">2Jn 1:11</reference>.
entries.d483e8a978d973344d03fa5e155254a4f73f456d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen53943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53944" type="x-p"/> Count it all joy - The word πειρασμος, which we translate temptation, signifies affliction, persecution, or trial of any kind; and in this sense it is used here, not intending diabolic suggestion, or what is generally understood by the word temptation.
entries.dd05387bfc55d241e4b604690a647f133e700cee: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen53944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53945" type="x-p"/> The trying of your faith - Trials put religion, and all the graces of which it is composed to proof; the man that stands in such trials gives proof that his religion is sound, and the evidence afforded to his own mind induces him to take courage, bear patiently, and persevere.
entries.205048a676c10090e1a502d24071ff78e0837ee8: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen53945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53946" type="x-p"/> Let patience have her perfect work - That is, Continue faithful, and your patience will be crowned with its full reward; for in this sense is εργον, which we translate work, to be understood. It is any effect produced by a cause, as interest from money, fruit from tillage, gain from labor, a reward for services performed; the perfect work is the full reward. See many examples in Kypke. <div eID="gen53946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53947" type="x-p"/> That ye may be perfect and entire - Τελειοι, Fully instructed, in every part of the doctrine of God, and in his whole will concerning you. Ὁλοκληροι, having all your parts, members, and portions; that ye may have every grace which constitutes the mind that was in Christ, so that your knowledge and holiness may be complete, and bear a proper proportion to each other. These expressions in their present application are by some thought to be borrowed from the Grecian games: the man was τελειος, perfect, who in any of the athletic exercises had got the victory; he was ὁλοκληρος, entire, having every thing complete, who had the victory in the pentathlon, in each of the five exercises. Of this use in the last term I do not recollect an example, and therefore think the expressions are borrowed from the sacrifices under the law. A victim was τελειος, perfect, that was perfectly sound, having no disease; it was ὁλοκληρος, entire, if it had all its members, having nothing redundant, nothing deficient. Be then to the Lord what he required his sacrifices to be; let your whole heart, your body, soul, and spirit, be sanctified to the Lord of hosts, that he may fill you with all his fullness.
