Thus the argument is from the end or the effect: hence we conclude, that the faithful are harassed by so many evils for this purpose, that their piety and obedience may be made manifest, and that they may be thus at length prepared to receive the crown of life.<div eID="gen136976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen136977" type="x-p"/>But they reason absurdly who hence infer that we by fighting merit the crown; for since God has gratuitously appointed it for us, our fighting only renders us fit to receive it.<div eID="gen136977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen136978" type="x-p"/>He adds, that it is <hi type="italic">promised</hi> to those who <hi type="italic">love</hi> God. By speaking thus, he means not that the love of man is the cause of obtaining the crown, (for God anticipates us by his gratuitous love;) but he only intimates that the elect who love him are alone approved by God. He then reminds us that the conquerors of all temptations are those who love God, and that we fail not in courage when we are tried, for no other cause than because the love of the world prevails in us.<div eID="gen136978" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen136974" osisID="Jas.1.12" type="section"/>
entries.f3a55618cbb60451c844cab251690919e9ad159e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jas.1.13" sID="gen136979" type="section"/> <div sID="gen136980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13</hi> <hi type="italic">Let no man, when he is tempted</hi>. Here, no doubt, he speaks of another kind of temptation. It is abundantly evident that the external temptations, hitherto mentioned, are sent to us by God. In this way God tempted Abraham, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.22.1">Genesis 22:1</reference>,) and daily tempts us, that is, he tries us as to what are we by laying before us an occasion by which our hearts are made known. But to draw out what is hid in our hearts is a far different thing from inwardly alluring our hearts by wicked lusts.<div eID="gen136980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen136981" type="x-p"/>He then treats here of inward temptations which are nothing else than the inordinate desires which entice to sin. He justly denies that God is the author of these, because they flow from the corruption of our nature.<div eID="gen136981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen136982" type="x-p"/>This warning is very necessary, for nothing is more common among men than to transfer to another the blame of the evils they commit; and they then especially seem to free themselves, when they ascribe it to God himself. This kind of evasion we constantly imitate, delivered down to us as it is from the first man. For this reason James calls us to confess our own guilt, and not to implicate God, as though he compelled us to sin.<div eID="gen136982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen136983" type="x-p"/>But the whole doctrine of scripture seems to be inconsistent with this passage; for it teaches us that men are blinded by God, are given up to a reprobate mind, and delivered over to filthy and shameful lusts. To this I answer, that probably James was induced to deny that we are tempted by God by this reason, because the ungodly, in order to form an excuse, armed themselves with testimonies of Scripture. But there are two things to be noticed here: when Scripture ascribes blindness or hardness of heart to God, it does not assign to him the beginning of this blindness, nor does it make him the author of sin, so as to ascribe to him the blame: and on these two things only does James dwell.<div eID="gen136983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen136984" type="x-p"/>Scripture asserts that the reprobate are delivered up to depraved lusts; but is it because the Lord depraves or corrupts their hearts? By no means; for their hearts are subjected to depraved lusts, because they are already corrupt and vicious. But since God blinds or hardens, is he not the author or minister of evil? Nay, but in this manner he punishes sins, and renders a just reward to the ungodly, who have refused to be ruled by his Spirit. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.1.26">Romans 1:26</reference>.) It hence follows that the origin of sin is not in God, and no blame can be imputed to him as though he took pleasure in evils. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.6.6">Genesis 6:6</reference>.)<div eID="gen136984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen136985" type="x-p"/>The meaning is, that man in vain evades, who attempts to cast the blame of his vices on God, because every evil proceeds from no other fountain than from the wicked lust of man. And the fact really is, that we are not otherwise led astray, except that every one has his own inclination as his leader and impeller. But that God tempts no one, he proves by this, because he is <hi type="italic">not tempted with evils</hi> <note n="105"> <div sID="gen136986" type="x-p"/> Literally, “untemptable by evils,” that is, not capable of being tempted or seduced by evils, by things wicked and sinful. He is so pure, that he is not influenced by any evil propensities, that he is not subject to any evil suggestions. It hence follows that he tempts or seduces no man to what is sinful. Being himself unassailable by evils, he cannot seduce others to what is evil. As God cannot be tempted to do what is sinful, he cannot possibly tempt others to sin. The words may thus be rendered, —<div eID="gen136986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen136987" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen136987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen136988" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13</hi>. “Let no one, when seduced, say, ‘By God I am seduced;’ for God is not capable of being seduced by evils, and he himself seduceth no one.”<div eID="gen136988" type="x-p"/> </note> For it is the devil who allures us to sin, and for this reason, because he wholly burns with the mad lust of sinning. But God does not desire what is evil: he is not, therefore, the author of doing evil in us.<div eID="gen136985" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen136979" osisID="Jas.1.13" type="section"/>
entries.ed492d298361b64180fc590e3356a3431c0ecf92: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.14" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jas.1.14" sID="gen136989" type="section"/> <div sID="gen136990" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">14</hi> <hi type="italic">When he is drawn away by his own lust.</hi> As the inclination and excitement to sin are inward, in vain does the sinner seek an cause from an external impulse. At the same time these two effects of lust ought to be noticed — that it ensnares us by its allurements, and that it does us away; each of which is sufficient to render us guilty. <note n="106"> <div sID="gen136991" type="x-p"/> The words are very striking, — “But every one is tempted (or, seduced) when, by his own lust, <hi type="italic">he is</hi> drawn away, (that is, from what is good,) and <hi type="italic">is</hi> caught by a bait (or, ensnared.)”<div eID="gen136991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen136992" type="x-p"/>He is in the first drawn off from the line of duty, and then he is caught by something that is pleasing and plausible, but like the bait, it has in it a deadly hook.<div eID="gen136992" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen136990" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.14" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen136989" osisID="Jas.1.14" type="section"/>
entries.48c993080a6f8e86b96215409454864e6fc81a0f:
15 Then when lust hath conceived. He first calls that lust which is not any kind of evil affection or desire, but that which is the fountain of all evil affections; by which, as he shews, are conceived vicious broods, which at length break forth into sins. It seems, however, improper, and not according to the usage of Scripture, to restrict the word sin to outward works, as though indeed lust itself were not a sin, and as though corrupt desires, remaining closed up within and suppressed, were not so many sins. But as the use of a word is various, there is nothing unreasonable if it be taken here, as in many other places, for actual sin.
And the Papists ignorantly lay hold on this passage, and seek to prove from it that vicious, yea, filthy, wicked, and the most abominable lusts are not sins, provided there is no assent; for James does not shew when sin begins to be born, so as to be sin, and so accounted by God, but when it breaks forth. For he proceeds gradually and shews that the consummation of sin is eternal death, and that sin arises from depraved desires, and that these depraved desires or affections have their root in lust. It hence follows that men gather fruit in eternal perdition, and fruit which they have procured for themselves.
By perfected sin, therefore, I understand, not any one act of sin perpetrated, but the completed course of sinning. For though death is merited by every sin whatever, yet it is said to be the reward of an ungodly and wicked life. Hence is the dotage of those confuted who conclude from these words, that sin is not mortal until it breaks forth, as they say, into an external act. Nor is this what James treats of; but his object was only this, to teach that there is in us the root of our own destruction.
James 1:16-18
16 Do not err, my beloved brethren.
16 Ne erretis, fratres mei dilecti:
17 Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.
17 Omnis donatio bona et omne donum perfectum desursum est, descendens a Patre luminum; apud quem non est transmutatio, aut conversionis obumbratio.
18 Of his own will begat he us with the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.
18 Is sua voluntate genuit nos veritatis, ut essemus primitiae quaedam suaram creaturarum.
entries.946151f42b2ca20e8e91cb05bd31b9fef0871de3: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.16" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jas.1.16" sID="gen137006" type="section"/> <div sID="gen137007" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">16</hi> <hi type="italic">Do not err</hi>. This is an argument from what is opposite; for as God is the author of all good, it is absurd to suppose him to be the author of evil. To do good is what properly belongs to him, and according to his nature; and from him all good things come to us. Then, whatever evil he does, is not agreeable to his nature. But as it sometimes happens, that he who quits himself well through life, yet in some things fails, he meets this doubt by denying that God is mutable like men. But if God is in all things and always like himself, it hence follows that well-doing is his perpetual work.<div eID="gen137007" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.16" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen137006" osisID="Jas.1.16" type="section"/>
entries.8b32fd5a7dc9860526b0d4859e7ab297b9fff918: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.17" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jas.1.17" sID="gen137008" type="section"/> <div sID="gen137009" type="x-p"/>This reasoning is far different from that of Plato, who maintained that no calamities are sent on men by God, because he is good; for though it is just that the crimes of men should be punished by God, yet it is not right, with regard to him, to regard among evils that punishment which he justly inflicts. Plato, indeed, was ignorant; but James, leaving to God his right and office of punishing, only removes blame from him. This passage teaches us, that we ought to be so affected by God’s innumerable blessings, which we daily receive from his hand, as to think of nothing but of his glory; and that we should abhor whatever comes to our mind, or is suggested by others, which is not compatible with his praise.<div eID="gen137009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137010" type="x-p"/>God is called the <hi type="italic">Father of lights</hi>, as possessing all excellency and the highest dignity. And when he immediately adds, that there is in him <hi type="italic">no shadow of turning</hi>, he continues the metaphor; so that we may not measure the brightness of God by the irradiation of the sun which appears to us. <note n="107"> <div sID="gen137011" type="x-p"/> This verse must be taken in connection with what as gone before. When he mentions “every good gift,” it is in opposition to the evil of which he says God is not the author. See <reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.7.11">Matthew 7:11</reference>. And “every perfect free-gift,” as <foreign xml:lang="el">δώρημα</foreign> means, has a reference to the correction of the evil which arises from man himself. And he calls free-gift perfect, because it has no mixture of evil, what he throughout denies that God is the author of. Then the latter part of the verse bears a correspondence with the first. He calls God “the Father of Lights.” Light in the language of scripture means especially two things, the light of truth, divine knowledge and holiness. God is the father, the parent, the origin, the source of these lights. Hence from him descends every good, useful, necessary gift, to deliver men from evil, from ignorance and delusion, and every perfect free-gift to free men from their evil lusts, and to render them holy and happy. And to shew that God is ever the same, he adds, “with whom there is no variableness or the shadow (or shade, of the slightest appearance) of a change;” that is, who never varies in his dealings with men, and shews no symptom of any change, being the author and giver of all good, and the author of no evil, that is, of no sin.<div eID="gen137011" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen137010" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.17" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen137008" osisID="Jas.1.17" type="section"/>
entries.826ad9aff0fe8aa15119cd9d9690953b2e0cbc82:
18 Of his own will. He now brings forward a special proof of the goodness of God which he had mentioned, even that he has regenerated us unto eternal life. This invaluable benefit every one of the faithful feels in himself. Then the goodness of God, when known by experience, ought to remove from them all a contrary opinion respecting him.
When he says that God of his own will, or spontaneously, hath begotten us, he intimates that he was induced by no other reason, as the will and counsel of God are often set in opposition to the merits of men. What great thing, indeed, would it have been to say that God was not constrained to do this? But he impresses something more, that God according to his own goodwill hath begotten us, and has been thus a cause to himself. It hence follows that it is natural to God to do good.
But this passage teaches us, that as our election before the foundation of the world was gratuitous, so we are illuminated by the grace of God alone as to the knowledge of the truth, so that our calling corresponds with our election. The Scripture shews that we have been gratuitously adopted by God before we were born. But James expresses here something more, that we obtain the right of adoption, because God does also call us gratuitously. (Ephesians 1:4, 5.) Farther, we hence learn, that it is the peculiar office of God spiritually to regenerate us; for that the same thing is sometimes ascribed to the ministers of the gospel, means no other thing than this, that God acts through them; and it happens indeed through them, but he nevertheless alone doeth the work.
The word begotten means that we become new men, so that we put off our former nature when we are effectually called by God. He adds how God begets us, even by the word of truth, so that we may know that we cannot enter the kingdom of God by any other door.
That we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures. The word τινὰ, “some,” has the meaning of likeness, as though he had said, that we are in a manner firstfruits. But this ought not to be restricted to a few of the faithful; but it belongs to all in common. For as man excels among all creatures, so the Lord elects some from the whole mass and separates them as a holy offering, to himself.
The firstfruits being a part and a pledge of the coming harvest, to retain the metaphor, we must regard “creatures” here as including all the saved in future ages. Hence their opinion is to be preferred, who regard the first converts, who were Jews, as the firstfruits.
It is no common nobility into which God extols his own children. Then justly are they said to be excellent as firstfruits, when God’s image is renewed in them.
James 1:19-21
19 Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
19 Itaque, fratres mei dilecti, sit omnis homo celer ad audiendum, tardus autem ad loquendum, tardus ad iram:
20 For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
20 Ira enim hominus justitiam Dei non operatur.
21 Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls.
21 Quapropter deposita omni inmunditie, et redundantia malitiae, cum mansuetudine suscipite insitum sermonem qui potest servare animas vestras.
entries.67fc11393cc02b29f7aed3f11c52f8ae6585c40c: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.19" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jas.1.19" sID="gen137028" type="section"/> <div sID="gen137029" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">19</hi> <hi type="italic"> Let every man</hi>. Were this a general sentence, the inference would be farfetched; but as he immediately adds a sentence respecting the word of truth suitable to the last verse, I doubt not but that he accommodates this exhortation peculiarly to the subject in hand. Having then set before us the goodness of God, he shews how it becomes us to be prepared to receive the blessing which he exhibits towards us. And this doctrine is very useful, for spiritual generation is not a work of one moment. Since some remnants of the old man ever abide in us, we must necessarily be through life renewed, until the flesh be abolished; for either our perverseness, or arrogance, or sloth, is a great impediment to God in perfecting in us his work. Hence, when James would have us to be <hi type="italic">swift to hear</hi>, he commends promptitude, as though he had said, “When God so freely and kindly presents himself to you, you also ought to render yourselves teachable, lest your slowness should cause him to desist from speaking.”<div eID="gen137029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137030" type="x-p"/>But inasmuch as we do not calmly hear God speaking to us, when we seem to ourselves to be very wise, but by our haste interrupt him when addressing us, the Apostle requires us to be silent, to be <hi type="italic">slow to speak</hi>. And, doubtless, no one can be a true disciple of God, except he hears him in silence. He does not, however, require the silence of the Pythagorean school, so that it should not be right to inquire whenever we desire to learn what is necessary to be known; but he would only have us to correct and restrain our forwardness, that we may not, as it commonly happens, unseasonably interrupt God, and that as long as he opens his sacred mouth, we may open to him our hearts and our ears, and not prevent him to speak.<div eID="gen137030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137031" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Slow to wrath</hi>. Wrath also, I think, is condemned with regard to the hearing which God demands to be given to him, as though making a tumult it disturbed and impeded him, for God cannot be heard except when the mind is calm and sedate. Hence, he adds, that as long as wrath bears rule there is no place for the righteousness of God. In short, except the heat of contention be banished, we shall never observe towards God that calm silence of which he has just spoken.<div eID="gen137031" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.19" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen137028" osisID="Jas.1.19" type="section"/>
entries.2d4d29900b28751bf53fd925b5b459a63ba13876:
21 Wherefore lay apart. He concludes by saying how the word of life is to be received. And first, indeed, he intimates that it cannot be rightly received except it be implanted, or strike roots in us. For the expression, to receive the implanted word, ought to be thus explained, “to receive it, that it may be really implanted.” For he alludes to seed often sown on and ground, and not received into the moist bosom of the earth; or to plants, which being cast on the ground, or laid on dead wood, soon wither. He then requires that it should be a living implanting, by which the word becomes as it were united with our heart.
He at the same time shews the way and manner of this reception, even with meekness. By this word he means humility and the readiness of a mind disposed to learn, such as Isaiah describes when he says,
“On whom does my Spirit rest, except on the humble and meek?” (Isaiah 57:15.)
Hence it is, that so far profit in the school of God, because hardly one in a hundred renounces the stubbornness of his own spirit, and gently submits to God; but almost all are conceited and refractory. But if we desire to be the living plantation of God, we must subdue our proud hearts and be humble, and labor to become like lambs, so as to suffer ourselves to be ruled and guided by our Shepherd.
But as men are never thus tamed, so as to have a calm and meek heart, except they are purged from depraved affections, so he bids us to lay aside uncleanness and redundancy of wickedness. And as James borrowed a comparison from agriculture, it was necessary for him to observe this order, to begin by rooting up noxious weeds. And since he addressed all, we may hence conclude that these are the innate evils of our nature, and that they cleave to us all; yea, since he addresses the faithful, he shews that we are never wholly cleansed from them in this life, but that they are continually sprouting up, and therefore he requires that care should be constantly taken to eradicate them. As the word of God is especially a holy thing; to be fitted to receive it, we must put off the filthy things by which we have been polluted.
Under the word κακία, he comprehends hypocrisy and obstinacy as well as unlawful desires or lusts. Not satisfied with specifying the seat of wickedness as being in the soul of man, he teaches us that so abounding is the wickedness that dwells there, that it overflows, or that it rises up as it were into a heap; and doubtless, whosoever will well examine himself will find that there is within him an immense chaos of evils.
What renders this passage unsatisfactory is the meaning given to περισσεία, rendered by some “superfluity,” and by others “redundancy.” The verb περισσεύω means not only to abound, but also to be a residue, to remain, to be a remnant. See Matthew 14:20; Luke 9:17. And its derivative περίσσευμα is used in the sense of a remnant or a remainder, Mark 8:8; and this very word is used in the Sept., for יתר which means a residue, a remnant, or what remains, Ezekiel 6:8. Let it have this meaning here, and the sense will not only be clear, but very striking. James was addressing those who were Christians; and he exhorted them to throw away every uncleanness and remnant of wickedness, or evil, as the word κακία more properly means. See Acts 8:22; 1 Peter 2:16
“Every uncleanness,” or filthiness, means every kind of uncleanness arising from lustful and carnal indulgences; and the “remnant of wickedness,” in thought and in deed, most suitably follows.
Which is able to save. It is a high eulogy on heavenly truth, that we obtain through it a sure salvation; and this is added, that we may learn to seek and love and magnify the word as a treasure that is incomparable. It is then a sharp goad to chastise our idleness, when he says that the word which we are wont to hear so negligently, is the means of our salvation, though for this purpose the power of saving is not ascribed to the word, as if salvation is conveyed by the external sound of the word, or as if the office of saving is taken away from God and transferred elsewhere; for James speaks of the word which by faith penetrates into the hearts of men, and only intimates that God, the author of salvation, conveys it by his Gospel.
James 1:22-27
22 But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
22 Estote factores sermones, et non auditores solum, fallentes vos ipsos.
23 For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass:
23 Nam si quis auditor est sermones, et non factor, hic similis est homini consideranti faciem nativitatis suae in speculo.
24 For he beholdeth himself, and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was.
24 Consideravit enim seipsum, et abiit, et protinus oblitus est qualis sit.
25 But whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty, and continueth therein, he being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed.
25 Qui vero intuitus fuerit in legem perfectam, quae est libertatis, et permanserit, hic non auditor obliviosus, sed factor operis, beatus in opere suo erit.
26 If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man’s religion is vain.
26 Si quis videtur religiosus esse inter vos, nec refraenat linguam suam, sed decipits cor suum, hujus inanus est religio.
27 Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
27 Religio pura et impolluta coram Deo et Patre, haec est, Visitare pupillos et viduas in afflictione ipsorum, inmaculatum servare se a mundo.
entries.e79dfee91ed3446036fac86c7f9be25516f290c3: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.22" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jas.1.22" sID="gen137057" type="section"/> <div sID="gen137058" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">22</hi> <hi type="italic">Be ye doers of the word</hi>. The doer here is not the same as in <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.2.13">Romans 2:13</reference>, who satisfied the law of God and fulfilled it in every part, but the doer is he who from the heart embraces God’s word and testifies by his life that he really believes, according to the saying of Christ,<div eID="gen137058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137059" type="x-p"/>“Blessed are they who hear God’s word and keep it,”<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.11.28">Luke 11:28</reference>;)<div eID="gen137059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137060" type="x-p"/>for he shews by the fruits what that implanting is, before mentioned. We must further observe, that faith with all its works is included by James, yea, faith especially, as it is the chief work which God requires from us. The import of the whole is, that we ought to labor that the word of the Lord should strike root in us, so that it may afterwards fructify. <note n="110"> <div sID="gen137061" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Calvin</hi> takes no notice of the last sentence, “deceiving yourselves.” The participle means deceiving by false reasoning.; it may be rendered with <hi type="italic">Doddridge</hi>, “sophistically deceiving yourselves.”<div eID="gen137061" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen137060" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.22" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen137057" osisID="Jas.1.22" type="section"/>
entries.003227425b939d309ce074d5ace3347a08541dbc: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.23" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jas.1.23" sID="gen137062" type="section"/> <div sID="gen137063" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">23</hi> <hi type="italic">He is like to a man</hi>. Heavenly doctrine is indeed a mirror in which God presents himself to our view; but so that we may be transformed unto his image, as Paul says in <reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.3.18">2 Corinthians 3:18</reference>. But here he speaks of the external glance of the eye, not of the vivid and efficacious meditation which penetrates into the heart. It is a striking comparison, by which he briefly intimates, that a doctrine merely heard and not received inwardly into the heart avails nothing, because it soon vanishes away.<div eID="gen137063" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.23" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen137062" osisID="Jas.1.23" type="section"/>
entries.2d71009e5ce0b0fa65aad1fb2f35578b126215da: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.25" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jas.1.25" sID="gen137064" type="section"/> <div sID="gen137065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">25</hi> <hi type="italic">The perfect law of liberty</hi>. After having spoken of empty speculation, he comes now to that penetrating intuition which transforms us to the image of God. And as he had to do with the Jews, he takes the word <hi type="italic">law</hi>, familiarly known to them, as including the whole truth of God.<div eID="gen137065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137066" type="x-p"/>But why he calls it <hi type="italic">a perfect law</hi>, and <hi type="italic">a law of liberty</hi>, interpreters have not been able to understand; for they have not perceived that there is here a contrast, which may be gathered from other passages of Scripture. As long as the law is preached by the external voice of man, and not inscribed by the finger and Spirit of God on the heart, it is but a dead letter, and as it were a lifeless thing. It is, then, no wonder that the law is deemed imperfect, and that it is the law of bondage; for as Paul teaches in <reference osisRef="Bible:Gal.4.24">Galatians 4:24</reference>, separated from Christ, it generates to condemn and as the same shews to us in <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.13">Romans 8:13</reference>, it can do nothing but fill us with diffidence and fear. But the Spirit of regeneration, who inscribes it on our inward parts, brings also the grace of adoption. It is, then, the same as though James had said, “The teaching of the law, let it no longer lead you to bondage, but, on the contrary, bring you to liberty; let it no longer be only a schoolmaster, but bring you to perfection: it ought to be received by you with sincere affection, so that you may lead a godly and a holy life.”<div eID="gen137066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137067" type="x-p"/>Moreover, since it is a blessing of the Old Testament that the law of God should reform us, as it appears from <reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.31.33">Jeremiah 31:33</reference>, and other passages, it follows that it cannot be obtained until we come to Christ. And, doubtless, he alone is the end and perfection of the law; and James adds <hi type="italic">liberty</hi>, as an inseparable associate, because the Spirit of Christ never regenerates but that he becomes also a witness and an earnest of our divine adoption, so as to free our hearts from fear and trembling.<div eID="gen137067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137068" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And continueth</hi>. This is firmly to persevere in the knowledge of God; and when he adds, <hi type="italic">this man shall be blessed in his deed</hi>, or work, he means that blessedness is to be found in doing, not in cold hearing. <note n="111"> <div sID="gen137069" type="x-p"/> It may be rendered thus, — “The same shall be blessed in (or by) the doing of it,” that is, the work. The very doing of the law of liberty, of what the gospel prescribes, makes a man blessed or happy.<div eID="gen137069" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen137068" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen137064" osisID="Jas.1.25" type="section"/>
entries.c31fc960222bbf40be6a842bd6372842b7f4bb84: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.26" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jas.1.26" sID="gen137070" type="section"/> <div sID="gen137071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">26</hi> <hi type="italic">Seem to be religious</hi>. He now reproves even in those who boasted that they were doers of the law, a vice under which hypocrites commonly labor, that is, the wantonness of the tongue in detraction. He has before touched on the duty of restraining the tongue, but for a different end; for he then bade silence before God, that we might be more fitted to learn. He speaks now of another thing, that the faithful should not employ their tongue in evil speaking.<div eID="gen137071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137072" type="x-p"/>It was indeed needful that this vice should be condemned, when the subject was the keeping of the law; for they who have put off the grosser vices, are especially subject to this disease. He who is neither an adulterer, nor a thief, nor a drunkard, but, on the contrary, seems brilliant with some outward shew of sanctity will set himself off by defaming others, and this under the pretense of zeal, but really through the lust of slandering.<div eID="gen137072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137073" type="x-p"/>The object here, then, was to distinguish between the true worshippers of God and hypocrites, who are so swollen with Pharisaic pride, that they seek praise from the defects of others. <hi type="italic">If any one,</hi> he says, <hi type="italic">seems to be religious,</hi> that is, who has a show of sanctity, and the meantime flatters himself by speaking evil of others, it is hence evident that he does not truly serve God. For by saying that his religion is vain, he not only intimates that other virtues are marred by the stain of evil-speaking, but that the conclusion is, that the zeal for religion which appears is not sincere.<div eID="gen137073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137074" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">But deceiveth his own heart</hi>. I do not approve of the version of Erasmus — “But suffers his heart to err;” for he points out the fountain of that arrogance to which hypocrites are addicted, through which, being blinded by an immoderate love of themselves, they believe themselves to be far better than they really are; and hence, no doubt, is the disease of slandering, because the wallet, as Aesop says in his Apologue, hanging behind, is not seen. Rightly, then, has James, wishing to remove the effect, that is, the lust of evil-speaking, added the cause, even that hypocrites flatter themselves immoderately. For they would be ready to forgive were they in their turn to acknowledge themselves to be in need of forgiveness. Hence the flatteries by which they deceive themselves as to their own vices, make them such supercilious censors of others.<div eID="gen137074" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jas.1.26" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen137070" osisID="Jas.1.26" type="section"/>
entries.67dfd9b370545317bfbd569a96b133880e151517:
27 Pure religion. As he passes by those things which are of the greatest moment in religion, he does not define generally what religion is, but reminds us that religion without the things he mentions is nothing; as when one given to wine and gluttony boasts that he is temperate, and another should object, and say that the temperate man is he who does not indulge in excess as to wine or eating; his object is not to express the whole of what temperance is, but to refer only to one thing, suitable to the subject in hand. For they are in vain religious of whom he speaks, as they are for the most part trifling pretenders.
James then teaches us that religion is not to be estimated by the pomp of ceremonies; but that there are important duties to which the servants of God ought to attend.
To visit in necessity is to extend a helping hand to alleviate such as are in distress. And as there are many others whom the Lord bids us to succor, in mentioning widows and orphans, he states a part for the whole. There is then no doubt but that under one particular thing he recommends to us every act of love, as though he had said, “Let him who would be deemed religious, prove himself to be such by self denial and by mercy and benevolence towards his neighbors.”
And he says, before God, to intimate that it appears in deed otherwise to men, who are led astray by external masks, but that we ought to seek what pleases him. By God and Father, we are to understand God who is a father.
CHAPTER 2
James 2:1-4
1 My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons.
1 Fratres mei, ne in acceptionabus personarum fidem habeatis Domini Jesu Christi ex opinione, (vel, gloriae.)
2 For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment;
2 Si enim ingressus fuerit in coetum vestrum vir aureos anulos gestans, veste indudus spliendida; ingressus autem fuerit et pauper in sordida veste;
3 And ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, and say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool:
3 Et respexeritis in cum qui vestem fert splendidam, et ei dixeritis, Tu sede hic honeste, et pauperi dixeritis, Tu sta illic, vel, Sede hic sub scabello pedum meorum;
4 Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts?
4 An non dijudicati eestis in vobisipsis, et facti judices malarum cogitationum?

And so both are true, that Tribulation, as <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> speaks, and Trial, as <ns0:hi>Iames,</ns0:hi> work Pa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tience, and Patience not a further Trial, but rather Discovery, or Experiment, or Approbation of what we are, which ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pears by nothing more, than by Patience under Sufferings.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 But let patience have <ns0:hi>her</ns0:hi> perfect work <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Effect, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> let it have its full Efficacy in you, both in making you absolutely subject to God's Will, and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stant to the end under all your Sufferings.</ns0:note>, that ye may be perfect and entire <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">That you may grow perfect in this Grace, as well as in others, and have the Image of Christ (to whom ye are to be conformed) completed in you.</ns0:note>, wanting no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Either not failing, not fainting in Trials, or not defective in any thing which is a needful part of Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stianity.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Prov. 2.3.</ns0:note> If <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>If,</ns0:hi> doth not imply a Doubt, but supposeth something which they themselves would grant; <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> That they did lack Wisdom, either in whole, or in part. It is, as if he had said, Since, or seeing ye lack, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> See the like, <ns0:hi>Mal.</ns0:hi> 1.6.</ns0:note> any of you lack wisdom <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Though this hold true of Wisdom taken more generally, yet Wisdom here is to be restrained, according to the Cir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cumstances of the Text, and taken for Wisdom or Skill to bear Afflictions, so as to rejoice in them.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Mat. 21.22. Mark 11.24. Luke 11.9. John 14.13. & 15.7. & 16.26.</ns0:note> let him ask of God <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">By believing, fervent Prayer.</ns0:note>, that giveth to all men <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Either to all sorts of Men, <ns0:hi>Iew,</ns0:hi> or Gen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tile, bond or free, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> or to all that so ask, as appears by the next Verse.</ns0:note> liberally <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>simply,</ns0:hi> Rom. 12.8. <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> with an open, free, large Heart, in opposition to the contracted, narrow Spirits of covetous Misers. Our Translation renders it well <ns0:hi>liberally</ns0:hi>; and so the word is used, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8.2. and 9, 13.</ns0:note>, and upbraideth not <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Doth not twit them with their Importunity, or Frequency in asking (as Men often do) however he may upbraid them with their Unthankfulness for, or abuse of what they have re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceived.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Jer. 29.12. 1 John 5.14.</ns0:note> it shall be given him <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Matth. 7.7, 8. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 16.23. The Promise is here added to encourage Faith in asking.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 But let him ask in faith <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">With Confidence of God's hearing, grounded on the Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vine Attributes and Promises, <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 11.24. and 1 <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 5.14.</ns0:note>, nothing waver<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Either not disputing God's Power or Promise; or rather, not doubting, not <ns0:hi>staggering through Vnbelief,</ns0:hi> Rom. 4.20. where the same <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word is used: So <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 10.20. <ns0:hi>no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing doubting</ns0:hi>; and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 11.23. where it is opposed to be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieving.</ns0:note>: For he that wavereth, is like a wave of the sea, driven with the wind, and tossed <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">This notes either the Emptiness, and Unprofitableness of faithless Prayer, when Men's Minds are thus at uncertain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties, tossed to and fro; the Confidence they sometimes seem to have, like Waves, falls down and fails, and their Prayers come to nothing: Or, the Disquiet, and Torment, Distrust works in the Minds of such Waverers, which are never set<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led, till Faith come and fix them, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 57.20.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 For let not that man <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">He that wavers, in opposition to him that asks in Faith: all doubting doth not hinder the hearing of Prayer, but that which excludes Faith, <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 9.23, 24.</ns0:note> think <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Vainly conceit, or perswade himself.</ns0:note> that he shall receive any thing <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Even the least Mercy, much less the Wisdom mentioned.</ns0:note> of the Lord</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 A double minded man <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Either, 1. an Hypocrite, who is said to have a double Heart, <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 12.2. Or, 2ly. rather he that is of a doubtful Mind, wavering, and fluctuating with contrary Motions, some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times of one Mind, sometimes of another; sometimes ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ping, sometimes desponding.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> unstable <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Either unconstant, without any fixedness, or Consistancy of Spirit; as ready to depart from God, as to cleave to him; or unquiet, troubled, full of in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward Tumults.</ns0:note> in all his ways <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">By an Hebraism, <ns0:hi>Ways,</ns0:hi> for Counsels, Pur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />poses, Actions, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 Let the brother <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The Believer, (for to such he writes.) all Belie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers, or Saints, being Brethren in Christ, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 16.20. and 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 5.26. and 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 6.2.</ns0:note> of low degree <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word signifies both lowliness of mind, and lowness of Condition (as the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> word doth, to which it answers) but here is to be understood of the latter (as <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 1.48.) but especially of such a low estate, as a Man is brought into for Christ's sake and the Gospels.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>glory.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> rejoice in that he is exalted <ns0:hi>k.</ns0:hi>
                  <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Either exalted to be a Brother, a Mem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ber of Christ, a Child of God, and Heir of Glory, which is the greatest Preferment, or exalted to the Honour of suf<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fering for Christ. See <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 5.41. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 5.3.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:573" />10 But the rich <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> Brother, he that is in an high, honourable, or plen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiful Condition in the World.</ns0:note> in that he is made low <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Supply from the former Verse, let him <ns0:hi>rejoyce in that he is made low</ns0:hi>; not as to his outward state (for he is supposed to be rich still) but his inward Disposition, and frame of Mind, God having given him a lowly Heart in an high Condition, and thereby prepared him for the Cross, tho as yet he be not under it</ns0:note>, because <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 14.2. Psal. 103.15. Isa. 40.6. 1 Cor. 7.31. 1 Pet. 1.24. 1 Joh. 2.17.</ns0:note> as the flower of the grass he shall pass away <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The Reason why the rich Brother should be humble in his greatest Abundance, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> because of the uncertainty of his enjoying what at present he possesseth; he is neither se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cure of his Life, nor his Wealth; he, and his Enjoyments pass away, and his Pomp vanisheth as easily as the Flower of the Grass, which fades as soon as it flourisheth.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 For the sun is <ns0:hi>no sooner</ns0:hi> risen with a burn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing heat <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Or, the scorching East-wind, which in those Countries was now to rise with the Sun, <ns0:hi>Io<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi> 4.8.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi> it withereth the grass, and the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth: so also shall the rich man <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Either <ns0:hi>shall</ns0:hi> is here put for <ns0:hi>may,</ns0:hi> the Future Tense for the Potential Mood, and then the Apostle doth not so much declare what always certainly shall be, as what easily may be, and frequently is, the Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sperity of Rich Men not being always of so short continu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ance. Or, <ns0:hi>shall,</ns0:hi> may be taken properly, as we read it, and then this is a general Proposition, shewing the muta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble Nature, and short continuance of Rich Men and their Ri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ches, whose longest Life is but short, and Death when it comes strips them of their Enjoyments; and tho this Frailty be common to all, yet he speaks of the Rich especially, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause they are so apt to bear themselves high upon their Wealth, and put Confidence in it, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 6.17.</ns0:note> fade away in his ways <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Either in his Journyings and Travels for his Riches, or rather in his Counsels, Purposes, Actions, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 146.4.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 5.17.</ns0:note> Blessed is the man that endureth <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Holds out against the Assaults and Impressions of Temp<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tations with Patience and Constancy, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 5.11. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 12.5, 7.</ns0:note> tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ptation <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Afflictions, as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 2.</ns0:note>, for when he is tried <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Approved, and found upon the Trial to be sound in the Faith: a Metaphor taken from Mettals tri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed by Fire, and found pure.</ns0:note>, he shall re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceive <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">1 Cor. 9.25. Chap. 2.5.</ns0:note> the crown of life <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">So the heavenly Glory is called, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 2.10. either because it is not to be had, but in eternal Life; or because of its Duration, and not fading a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />way, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 5.4.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Mat. 10.22. and 19, 28, 29.</ns0:note> which the Lord hath promised <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">This shews on what ground it is to be expected, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> on the account of the Promise, and how sure we may be of it.</ns0:note> to them that love him <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> All true Believers, whose Faith, and thereby Title to the Crown is evidenced by Love, which is the fulfilling of the Law. <ns0:hi>Object.</ns0:hi> Why not promised to them that suffer for Christ, of whom he here speaks? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> That is implied, for none l<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ve him more, or evidence their Love to him more than they that suffer for him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 Let no man say <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Neither with his Mouth, nor so much as in his Heart blasphemously cast the blame of his Sins upon God, to clear himself.</ns0:note> when he is tempted <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">So stirred up to sin, as to be drawn to it.</ns0:note>, I am tempted of God <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther sollicited by God to sin, or enforced to it.</ns0:note>: For God cannot be tempted with <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>E<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ils.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> evil <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Cannot be drawn aside to any thing that is unrighteous, by any motion from within, or Impression from without.</ns0:note>, neither tempteth he any man <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Doth no way seduce, or enforce to sin, so as to be justly chargeable, as the Author of it. <ns0:hi>Object.</ns0:hi> God is said to be tempted, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 17.2, 7. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 6.16. <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 78.41. and to tempt, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 22.1. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 8.2. and 13.3. <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> Both are to be understood of Temptations of Exploration, or for the Discovery of some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing that was before hidden. Men tempt God, that they may know what he will do: God tempts Men, that they (not he, for he knows it already) may know what them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves will do, which then appears, when the Temptation draws it out; but neither is to be understood of the Tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ptation here spoken of, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> of Seduction, or drawing into <ns0:hi>Sin.</ns0:hi> God tempts by giving hard Commands, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 22.1. by afflicting, as in <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi>'s case, by letting loose Satan, or other wicked Instruments to tempt, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 22.22. by with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />holding his Grace, and deserting Men, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 28.15. by presenting Occasions, which Corruption within improves unto Sin, and by ordering and governing the evil Wills of Men; as that a Thief should steal out of this Flock, rather than that; that <ns0:hi>Nebuchadnezzar</ns0:hi> should rather come against <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> than <ns0:hi>Rabbah,</ns0:hi> Ezek. 21.21, 22. But God doth not tempt by commanding, suggesting, solli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />citing, or perswading to sin.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 But every man is tempted <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">He shews the great cause of Sin; that Lust hath a greater hand in it, than either the Devil, or his Instruments, who cannot make us <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>in without our selves: They sometimes tempt, and do not prevail; but when Lust tempts, it always pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vails either in whole, or in part, it being a Degree of Sin to be our own Tempters.</ns0:note> when he is drawn away <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Either this notes a Degree of Sin, the Hearts being drawn off from God, or the way where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />by Lust brings into Sin, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> the Impetuousness and Violence of its motions in us.</ns0:note> of his own lust <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Original Corruption in its whole Latitude, tho chiefly with respect to the appetitive Faculties</ns0:note>
                  <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and enticed <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Either a farther degree of Sin <ns0:hi>enticed</ns0:hi> by the pleasantness of the Object, as represented by our own Corruption, or ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther way of Lusts working in us to sin, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> by the Delight<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fulness and Pleasure of its motions: In the former it works by a kind of force, in this by Flatery and Deceit. It is ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther a Metaphor taken from a Fish enticed by a Bait, and drawn after it, or rather from an Harlot drawing a young Man out of the right Way, and alluring him with the Bait of Pleasure to commit Folly with her.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 Then when lust hath conceived <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Lust (compared to an Harlot) may be said to conceive, when the Heart is pleased with the motion, and yields some con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent to it.</ns0:note>, it bringeth forth <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The Birth of Sin may be the complete consent of the Will to it, or the outward act of it.</ns0:note> sin, and sin <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Actual Sin the Fruit and Product of Original.</ns0:note> when it is finish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Sin is finished, when it is not only committed, but continued in, as the Way and Course of a Man's Life.</ns0:note>, bringeth forth death <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Not only temporal, but eternal: Or we may thus take the Order and Progress of Sin: The first indeliberate motion of Lust, is the Temptation or Bait, which by its Plea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />santness <ns0:hi>enticeth,</ns0:hi> and by its Vehemency <ns0:hi>draws</ns0:hi> the Heart after it (as the Harlot, <ns0:hi>Pro.</ns0:hi> 7.21. with the flattering of her Lips forced the young Man, telling him of the Pleasure he should enjoy, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 14, 16, 17, 18. and then he goes after her, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 22.) the Hearts lingring about, and being entangled with the de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lightful motion of Lust, is its committing Folly with it, when the full consent is joined, Lust hath <ns0:hi>conceived</ns0:hi>; when the out<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward Act is performed, Sin is <ns0:hi>brought forth</ns0:hi>; and when Sin is finished in a setled Course, it brings forth Death; which, tho every Sin do in the merit of it, yet Sin only <ns0:hi>finished,</ns0:hi> doth in the Event. <ns0:hi>Object.</ns0:hi> Doth not this imply Lust, and its first motions not to be Sin? <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> No: for, 1. the least motions of it are forbidden, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.28. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 7.7. 2ly. It is contrary to the Law and Spirit of God, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 7.23, 25. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 5.16, 17. 3ly. It is the Fountain of Impurity, and therefore is it self impure, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 14.4. <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 7.15, 16. <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> 3.11. 4ly. Evil Thoughts defile a Man, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 15.19. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 8.22. <ns0:hi>Obj.</ns0:hi> How is Lust said here to bring forth Sin, when <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 7.8. Sin is said to work Lust? <ns0:hi>Ans. Iames</ns0:hi> calls the corrupt Principle it self, Lust, and the actings of it, Sins; whereas <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> calls the same Principle, <ns0:hi>Sin,</ns0:hi> and the actings of it, Lusts. And so both are true, Lust, as a Root, brings forth the acts of Sin as its Fruit s; and Sin, as a Root, brings forth actual Lusts, as its Fruits.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 Do not err <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> in imputing your Sins to God, and saying, that when you are tempted, you are tempted of him.</ns0:note> my beloved brethren.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 4.7.</ns0:note>
                  <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Gr. <ns0:hi>giving,</ns0:hi> and so it may be distinct from <ns0:hi>Gift</ns0:hi> in the next clause; to shew, that whereas Men sometimes give good Gifts in an evil way, and with an evil Mind, God's <ns0:hi>giving,</ns0:hi> as well as Gift, is always good; and therefore when we re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceive any thing of him, we should look not only to the thing it self, but to his Bounty and Goodness in giving it: Or, it may be rendred as our Translators do, <ns0:hi>Gift,</ns0:hi> and so the word is sometimes used by profane Writers themselves; and then tho it may be implied, that all good Gifts, and of all kinds, of Nature, and of Grace, are from God, yet the Apostle's Design in this place being to prove, that God is not the Author of Sin; <ns0:hi>Good Gifts</ns0:hi> may most fairly be understood the best Gifts, those of Grace (spiritual Blessings, <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 1.3.) such being contrary to Sin, and destructive of it, in one of which he instanceth, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> Regeneration, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 18.</ns0:note> Every good gift, and every perfect gift <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The highest degree of good Gifts, those that perfect us most, to intimate, that all the Parts and Steps of spiri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tual Life, from the first beginning of Grace in Regenera<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, to the Consummation of it in Glory, are of God.</ns0:note>, is from above <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">i. e. From Heaven, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 3.27, 31. and Heaven is put for God that dwells there, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 15.21.</ns0:note>, and cometh down from the Father <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The Creator, Au<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thor, or first Cause, as <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 12.9. It is spoken after the manner of the <ns0:hi>Hebrews</ns0:hi>; See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 4.20, 21.</ns0:note> of lights <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">God is the Author of all Perfection, and so of corporeal Light; but here we are to understand spiritual Light, the Light of Knowledge, Faith, Holiness, as opposed to the Darkness of Ignorance, Unbelief, Sin, of which he cannot be the Au<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thor.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Mal. 3.6.</ns0:note> with whom is no va<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />riableness, neither shadow of turning <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">He here sets forth God as essentially and immu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tably Good, and the Father of Lights, by allusion to the Sun the Fountain of corporeal light, and makes use of terms borrowed from Astronomy. The Sun though it scattereth its Beams every where, yet is not without its Changes, Parallaxes, and diversities of Aspects, not onely sometimes clear, and sometimes eclipsed, but one while in the East, another in the South, then in the West; nor without its turnings in its annual course from Tropick to Tropick (to which the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word here used seems to allude) its va<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rious accesses and recesses, by reason of which it casts dif<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ferent shadows; but God is always the same, like himself constant in the emanations of his goodness, without cast<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing any dark shadow of evil which might infer a change in him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:573" />18 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 3.3.</ns0:note> Of his own will <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Out of his meer good pleasure as the Original cause, and not moved to it by any dignity or merit in us, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.9. and 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.9.</ns0:note> begat <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">By a spiritual generation, whereby we are new-born, and are made partakers of a Divine Nature. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 1.13. and 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.3, 23.</ns0:note> he us with the word of truth <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The Word of the Gospel, as the instrument or means whereby we are rege<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nerated: Why it is called the Word of Truth, see <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.13.</ns0:note>, that we should be a kind of first fruits <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Most excellent Creatures, being singled out and se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />parated from the rest, and consecrated to God, as under the Law the first-Fruits were, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 14.4.</ns0:note> of his creatures <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> reasona<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble Creatures; the word Creature being elsewhere restrain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed to Men. See <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 16.15. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.15.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 Wherefore, my beloved brethren, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eccles. 5.1.</ns0:note> let every man be swift to hear <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Prompt and ready to hear God speaking in the word of Truth before mentioned.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Prov. 17.27.</ns0:note> slow to speak <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Either silently and submis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sively hear the Word, or speak not rashly and precipitate<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly of the things of Faith, but be well furnished your selves with Spiritual knowledg, ere you take upon you to <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>each others.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Eccles. 7.9.</ns0:note> slow to wrath <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Either be not angry at the Word, or the Dispen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sers of it, though it come close to your Consciences, and discover your secret Sins; the word is Salt, do not quar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rel if it make your Sores smart, being it will keep them from festering: or, be not angrily prejudiced against those that dissent from you.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 For the wrath of man <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">That anger which is meerly humane, and generally sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful inordinate passion, and carnal zeal</ns0:note> worketh not the righteousness of God <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">will not acomplish the ends of the Word in you, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> to work that righteous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, which in the Word God prescribes you. But here is withall a <ns0:hi>Meiosis</ns0:hi> in the Words, less being spoken than is intended; it is implied therefore, that the wrath of Man hinders the operation of the Word, and disposeth to that unrighteousness which is forbidden by it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 Wherefore lay apart <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Not only restrain it, and keep it in; but put off, and throw it away as a filthy rag, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 30.22. see <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 4.22. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.8. and 1 Pet. 2.1.</ns0:note> all <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Of every kind.</ns0:note> filthiness <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>sordid<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness</ns0:hi>; a Metaphor borrowed from the filth of the Body, 1 Pet. 3.21. and thence transferred to the Soul; and it here seems to imply not only Sensuality or Covetousness, but all sorts of Lusts, whereby Men are defiled, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 7.1. and 2 Pet. 2.20.</ns0:note> and superfluity <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> That naughtiness which is super<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fluous: That is said to be superfluous or redundant, which is more than should be in a thing; in which respect all Sin is superfluous in the Soul, as being that which should not be in it; and so this intimates that we are not only to lay apart more gross pollutions, but all the Lusts of the Flesh, and relicts of old <ns0:hi>Adam,</ns0:hi> as being all superfluities which may well be spared, or excrements (as some ren<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the word agreeably to the former Metaphor) which should be cast away.</ns0:note> of naughtiness, and receive <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Not only into your Heads by Knowledg, but into your Hearts by Faith.</ns0:note> with meekness <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">With humi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lity, modesty and gentleness, which makes Men submissive to the truth of the Word, and ready to learn of God e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven those things which are above their natural capacity, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 25.9. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 66.2. <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 11.5, 27. this is opposed to <ns0:hi>Wrath</ns0:hi> which makes Men unteachable.</ns0:note> the engraffed <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Either which is engrafted or implanted, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> Ministerially by the Preachers of the Gospel, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.6, 7. principally by the Spirit of God, who writes it in the heart, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 31.33. And thus it may be taken particularly for the Word of the Gospel, in opposition to the Law which came to Mens ears from without, and admonished them o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> their Duty, but was not wri<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> in their hearts, or engrafted thereto from them unto obedience to it. Or, <ns0:hi>that it may be engraffed, i. e.</ns0:hi> Intimate<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly united to, or rooted in the heart by a vital union, or made natural to it (as some render the word) the heart being transformed by the power of it, and conformed to the Precepts of it, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.18. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 6.17.</ns0:note> word which <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> when received by Faith.</ns0:note> is able to save <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Instrumentally, as being the means wherein God puts forth his power in saving them, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.16.</ns0:note> your souls <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Your selves, the Soul as the noblest part, is by by a Synecdoche, put for the whole person. See 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.9.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 7.21, 22. Rom. 2.13.</ns0:note> But be ye doers of the word <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The same as doers of <ns0:hi>the Work,</ns0:hi> v. 25. namely, which the Word prescribes, <ns0:hi>q.d.</ns0:hi> receive the Word by Faith into your Hearts, and bring forth the fruit of it in your Lives; see <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 11.28. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 13.17.</ns0:note>, and not hearers only <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Not contenting your selves with a bare hearing the Word, though it have no influ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ence upon you.</ns0:note> deceiving your own selves <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Playing the Sophisters with, or putting a fallacy upon your selves, particularly perswading your selves into a good opinion of your state, meerly because of your being hearers of the Word, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 7.21.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 6.47. &c. See chap. 2.14. &c.</ns0:note> if any man be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word here used, properly signifies the Sex, not the Species, but is indifferently used by this Apostle with the other, as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 12, and 20. so that by a Man look<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing his Face in a Glass, is meant any Man or Woman.</ns0:note> be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />holding his natural face <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>the face of his Nativity</ns0:hi> by an Hebraism, for natural Face, as we translate it, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> his own Face, that which Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture gave him, or he was born with.</ns0:note> in a glass <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The Word is here compared to a Looking-Glass; as the Glass represents to us the Features and Complexions of our Faces, whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther beautiful or deformed; so the Word shews us the true face of our Souls, the beauty of God's Image when restored to them, and the Spots of Sin which so greatly disfigure them.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 For he beholdeth himself, and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The remembrance of what his Face is, vanisheth as soon as his Eye is off the Glass; he remembers not the Spots he saw in his Face to wipe them off. So he that sees the Blemishes of his Soul, in the Glass of the Word, and doth not remember them to do them away; looks in that Glass (<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> hears the Word) in vain.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 But whoso looketh <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> intently and earnestly, searching diligently into the Mind of God. The Word signifies a bowing down of the Head to look into a thing; and is used of the Disciples looking into Christ's Sepulcher, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 24.12. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 20.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. see 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.12. and seems to be opposed to looking into a Glass, which is more slight, and without such prying and inquisitiveness.</ns0:note> into the perfect <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 2.12.</ns0:note> law of liberty <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The whole Doctrine of the Scripture, or especially the Gospel called a Law, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 3.27. both as it is a Rule, and by reason of the Power it hath over the Heart; and a Law of Liberty, because it shews the way to the best Liberty, freedom from Sin, the Bondage of the Ceremonial Law, the rigour of the Moral, and from the Wrath of God; and likewise the way of serving God freely and ingenuously as Children; and because being re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceived into the Heart, it is accompanied with the Spirit of Adoption who works this Liberty, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.17. It is called a perfect Law, not only as being intire and without any defect, but as directing us to the greatest Perfection, full conformity to God, and enjoyment of him, 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 3.16, 17.</ns0:note>, and continueth <ns0:hi>therein</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Perseveres in the study, belief, and obedience of this Doctrine, (<ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 1.2.) in a l conditions, a nd under all temptations and afflictions. This seems to be opposed to him, who, when he hath looked in a Glass, <ns0:hi>goes away, v.</ns0:hi> 24. By which are set forth flight, superficial hearers, who do not continue in Christ's Word, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 8.31.</ns0:note>, he be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing not a forgetful hearer <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Gr. <ns0:hi>hear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />er of forgetfulness,</ns0:hi> by an Hebraism for a forgetful Hearer; it answers to him in the former Verse, that <ns0:hi>forgets what man<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ner of Man he was</ns0:hi>; and implies, not only, not remembring the Truths we have heard, but a not practising them, as appears by the next Clause.</ns0:note> but a doer of the work <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> which the Word di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rects him to do: The Singular Number is put for the Plural; he means, he that reduceth what he hears into practice, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 103.18.</ns0:note>, this <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Joh. 13.17.</ns0:note> man shall be blessed in his <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>doing.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> deed <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">This is opposed to bare hear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, and the doer of the Work is said to be blessed in, or by his Deed, as the evidence of his present begun Blessedness, and the way to his future perfect Happi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 If any man among you seem <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Seems to others, or rather to himself; thinks himself religious, because of his hearing and outward Worship; thus the Word rendred <ns0:hi>seems,</ns0:hi> is often taken, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.18. and 8.2. and 14.37. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.3. Here he shews who are not <ns0:hi>do<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>rs of the Work,</ns0:hi> as in the next Verse, who are.</ns0:note> to be religious, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 34.13. and 39.1. 1 Pet. 3.10.</ns0:note> bridleth not his tongue <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />strains it not from the common Vices of the Tongue, re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viling, railing, censuring, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, but deceiveth his own heart <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Either deceiveth his own heart in thinking himself Religious, when indulging him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self in things so contrary to Religion, or deceives his own heart, being blinded with self-love, and lifted up with self-conceit, which is the cause of his censuring, and speaking evil of others.</ns0:note>, that man's religion <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> vain <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Empty and to no purpose, having no reality in it self, and bringing no benefit to him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:574" />27 Pure <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">True, sinccre, genuine, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.8. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 15.3.</ns0:note> religion and undefiled <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">This seems to reflect upon the Hypocritical <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> whose Religion consisted so much in external observances, and keeping themselves from Ceremonial Defilements, when yet they were sullied with so many moral ones, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 14. <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 23.23. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 18.28. devoured Widows Houses. They thought their Religion pure and undefiled; the Apostle shews here which is really so</ns0:note> before God <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">in the sight of God, and according to his Judgment.</ns0:note> and the Father <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> God who is the Father, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> being only explicative, as <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.3. and 5.20. yet this Title may be given here to God with respect to what follows; and to shew that such acts of Charity are acceptable to him that is called <ns0:hi>the Iudg of Widows, and the Father of the Fatherless,</ns0:hi> Psal. 68.5.</ns0:note> is this, To visit <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">This includes all other acts of Charity to them, comforting, counselling, relieving them, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> the fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />therless and widdows <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">He doth not exclude others from being the objects of our Charity and Compassion, but instanceth in Fatherless and Widows, as being usually most miserable, because destitute of those relations which might be most helpful to them; and possibly in those times Persecution might encrease the number of Widows and Orphans.</ns0:note> in their affliction <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">When they had most need; lest any should think it sufficient to visit them that were rich, or in a prosperous condition.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> to keep himself unspotted of the world <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Untainted by the evil example of Men in the World, and free from the Lusts of the World, moral Pollutions. The Apostle doth not here define Religion, but only instanceth in these two things, good works, and holiness of conversation, as testi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monies and arguments of the truth of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
